s.x: **Purpose:** To offer reflection on the issue of human suffering, primarily by questioning the oft-held connection between moral goodness and prosperity
**Setting:** The patriarchal period, possibly in the land of Edom

i.x: When suffering comes to us, we often ask why. People sometimes say it’s because the sufferer did something wrong. The book of Job examines the suffering of one man who suffered precisely *because* he was blameless. Job’s friends supposed that he was guilty of some unknown sin. They tried to persuade him to repent, but Job knew he hadn’t sinned, so he questioned God. Finally, God appeared, but he did not give Job the answers he sought. Instead, God confronted Job, changed his perspective, and blessed him.
Setting

The book of Job unfolds early in the patriarchal age, before Israel became a nation. Job’s wealth, like Abraham’s, was in livestock and slaves ([1:3](Job.1.3); [42:12](Job.42.12); see [Gen 12:16](Gen.12.16); [32:5](Gen.32.5)). He was his family’s priest, as was a common practice before the law of Moses ([1:5](Job.1.5); [42:8](Job.42.8); see [Gen 4:4](Gen.4.4); [8:20](Gen.8.20); [12:7-8](Gen.12.7-Gen.12.8); [13:18](Gen.13.18); [15:9-10](Gen.15.9-Gen.15.10); [26:25](Gen.26.25); [33:20](Gen.33.20); [35:1-6](Gen.35.1-Gen.35.6); [46:1](Gen.46.1)). During Job’s time, the Sabeans and Chaldeans were nomadic raiders ([1:15](Job.1.15), [17](Job.1.17)), not important political and economic powers as in the late monarchical period (cp. [Isa 45:14](Isa.45.14); [Joel 3:8](Joel.3.8)). The money used by Job and his relatives was called the *kesitah*, which was used during the patriarchal age ([42:11](Job.42.11); see [Gen 33:19](Gen.33.19); [Josh 24:32](Josh.24.32)). Only those who lived before the flood ([Gen 1–6](Gen.1.1-Gen.6.22)) and the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) matched or exceeded Job’s longevity ([42:16](Job.42.16); see [Gen 5:3-32](Gen.5.3-Gen.5.32); [25:7](Gen.25.7); [35:28](Gen.35.28); [47:28](Gen.47.28); [50:26](Gen.50.26)). With Job, we return to the beginning of history, when mortals first struggled to know God and understand the world.
Summary

The prose introduction to the book of Job ([chs 1–2](Job.1.1-Job.2.13)) provides the heavenly perspective on Job’s suffering and sets the context for the human dialogue that forms most of the work. Job was a righteous man whom God allowed Satan to test. In the heavenly courtroom, Satan argued that if God removed his blessings from Job, he would “surely curse you to your face” ([1:11](Job.1.11)). Instead, Job responded, “Praise the name of the LORD!” ([1:21](Job.1.21)), and, “Should we accept only good things from the hand of God and never anything bad?” ([2:10](Job.2.10)). God’s praise for Job was vindicated.

The reader then leaves the court of heaven and enters the council of humans as three of Job’s friends come to sympathize with him. Their silent, seven-day vigil is apparently a genuine attempt to console Job ([2:11-13](Job.2.11-Job.2.13)). However, when Job breaks his silence with a bitter complaint ([ch 3](Job.3.1-Job.3.26)), his counselors begin to criticize and condemn him. In three rounds of debate ([chs 4–27](Job.4.1-Job.27.23)), their rhetoric varies from innuendo to blatant accusation. Job’s friends argue a tight theological case: Since God is righteous, he rewards each person according to what that person has done; therefore, Job’s suffering must be the just punishment for some evil he has committed. Job responds to each of their speeches by insisting that he is innocent and that his suffering is undeserved and unfair.

After the three rounds of dialogue between Job and his friends, a poetic interlude praises God as the sole source of wisdom (ch [28](Job.28.1-Job.28.28)). When Job then makes his final statement about both his misery and his righteousness (chs [29–31](Job.29.1-Job.31.40)), his three friends give up on him ([32:1](Job.32.1)). Elihu, a new voice, then renews the human struggle to explain Job’s suffering (chs [32–37](Job.32.1-Job.37.24)). Finally, God arrives to challenge Job (chs [38–41](Job.38.1-Job.41.34)). Instead of hearing Job’s case, God demands answers and poses questions that demonstrate his own power and sovereignty. Job responds with repentance and acknowledges that he does not have the right to question God ([42:1-6](Job.42.1-Job.42.6)).
In the final prose section ([42:7-17](Job.42.7-Job.42.17)), God reaffirms Job’s righteousness and faithfulness, pronounces judgment on Job’s friends, and pours out tremendous blessings on Job.
Job as History

The heavenly setting of the book’s opening and the manifestation of the supernatural at its closing tempt the modern reader to cast the book of Job as a fictional parable. The poetic dialogues also suggest that it is something more than just a dry historical record. But history can be described in flights of poetry just as well as in detailed narrative (cp. [Exod 14:21-31](Exod.14.21-Exod.14.31); [15:1-12](Exod.15.1-Exod.15.12); [Pss 78](Ps.78.1-Ps.78.72); [105](Ps.105.1-Ps.105.45)). The biblical record elsewhere suggests that the account of Job is historical. Both Ezekiel and James referred to Job as an example of righteousness and endurance ([Ezek 14:14](Ezek.14.14), [20](Ezek.14.20); [Jas 5:11](Jas.5.11)).
Author and Date of Composition

The authorship and composition of Job is a riddle. Although the story has a patriarchal setting (around 2000 BC), the date of its composition appears to be much later. Commentators have suggested dates that range from the era of Israel’s wilderness wanderings ([Exodus—Numbers](Exod.1.1-Num.36.13)) to the era following the return from exile ([Ezra—Nehemiah](Ezra.1.1-Neh.13.31)). The final composition of Job probably took place during the monarchy ([1–2 Kings](1Kgs.1.1-2Kgs.25.30)), when other wisdom materials such as [Proverbs](Prov.1.1-Prov.31.31) and [Ecclesiastes](Eccl.1.1-Eccl.12.14) were being accumulated.

Even if we accept that Job was a historical character, we still do not know who the author was, where he lived, or what level of society he came from. The author appears to have been a sage who was skilled in the use of proverbs (e.g., [4:2](Job.4.2); [6:5-6](Job.6.5-Job.6.6)), rhetorical questions (e.g., [21:29](Job.21.29)), and the art of eloquence. He also knew about plant and animal life, foreign culture, and antiquity, including the patriarchal period.

The book cannot be dated with certainty by reference to (1) events or people mentioned or implied in the book (the earliest reference to Job is during the Exile, [Ezek 14:14](Ezek.14.14), [20](Ezek.14.20)); (2) theological ideas in the book that point to distinct dates; or (3) its textual relationship to other material in the Old Testament (e.g., cp. [3:3-10](Job.3.3-Job.3.10); [Jer 20:14-18](Jer.20.14-Jer.20.18)). Job may even have been edited over a period of time by a number of different people.
Literary Characteristics

**Ancient Parallels to Job.**  The book of Job has several parallels in ancient Near Eastern literature (The following list of parallels is based on James B. Pritchard, ed., *Ancient Near Eastern Texts Relating to the Old Testament* , 3rd ed. \[Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1969\]):
• The Canaanite “Legend of King Keret” tells of a king who loses his family in a series of natural disasters; his god El restores his family.

• The Egyptian document “Dispute over Suicide” (2000s BC) tells of a man who considers suicide and hopes that someone will take up his case with the heavenly council. (Job wishes he had never been born, but he never considers suicide.)

• Also from Egypt, “Protests of the Eloquent Peasant” (2200s BC) tells the story of a robbery victim who is not treated justly and appeals to local authorities. At first he is polite, but as he keeps presenting his case, his language becomes increasingly strident.

• From Babylonia, the story “I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom” tells of a pious man of high rank who is struck with illness and mocked by friends. Unlike Job, this man believes that he has committed some accidental sin, perhaps something that he never thought was wrong. Rather than maintain his innocence, he acknowledges his guilt and begs for mercy. After a series of exorcisms that bring healing, his god restores his fortunes. In gratitude, he concludes with a long hymn of praise to his god.

• Also from Babylonia, the “Babylonian Theodicy” follows the same dialogue form that the book of Job uses: The sufferer complains, and his friends respond with rebukes. The arguments on both sides are remarkably similar to those in Job. Yet we also see key differences: (1) The “Babylonian Theodicy” is polytheistic, whereas Job is monotheistic; (2) its sufferer threatens to abandon his faith and give up obedience, even as he ends with a petition to his god and goddess. Job remains committed to the Lord throughout (e.g., [Job 13:15-16](Job.13.15-Job.13.16)).

**Relationship to Israel’s Wisdom Literature.**  The book of Job has the flavor of other works of Old Testament wisdom literature. Job’s friends follow lines of thought spelled out in Deuteronomy, Chronicles, and Proverbs. They argue that wisdom and righteousness lead to life and prosperity, while folly and wickedness lead to death and failure. Job joins the author of Ecclesiastes in questioning the simplistic, universal application of this doctrine.
Meaning and Message

The book of Job does not explain suffering. That is not its purpose. But it does demonstrate that suffering is not necessarily God’s retribution for sin. Job does not get an answer as to why bad things happen to good people, and neither do we.

The central conflict of the book is between the integrity of the Creator and the integrity of a man. Heaven and earth appear to be at odds. It is too easy simply to line up with Job’s three friends in denying Job’s innocence, as we can appeal to various New Testament passages that deny that any human is righteous (e.g., [Rom 3:10](Rom.3.10), [23](Rom.3.23); [Luke 18:19](Luke.18.19)). Job’s righteousness is genuine and thorough, though his obsession with his own rectitude sometimes borders on self-righteousness. He grows so adamant in defending his integrity that he seems ready to defy God. Job’s three friends set out a view of God that is more orthodox, at least on the surface. These counselors are more than weak, imaginary straw men; they accurately develop most of the biblical ways of explaining suffering. But their presumptuous applications go sour. They insist on a *quid pro quo* view of retribution, in which all the good and evil that people experience is directly related to what they have earned or deserved.

The book works within the basic commitments of Old Testament Israel’s faith. Job and all of the other speakers take seriously the covenantal ideas of blessing and cursing ([Lev 26](Lev.26.1-Lev.26.46); [Deut 28](Deut.28.1-Deut.28.68)) and of sowing and reaping in this life ([Ps 34:11-22](Ps.34.11-Ps.34.22); see also [Gal 6:7](Gal.6.7); [1 Pet 3:10](1Pet.3.10)). They don’t even consider solutions to the problem of why God permits the righteous to suffer (*theodicy*) from outside the scope of biblical revelation (e.g., metaphysical dualism, polytheistic tensions, or materialistic naturalism). Instead, the book’s speakers explore only biblical answers. They explain the meaning of suffering as (1) punishment for sin (e.g., [Job 4:7-9](Job.4.7-Job.4.9)); (2) the inevitable lot of mortals, who tend toward sin (e.g., [15:14-16](Job.15.14-Job.15.16)); (3) God’s discipline (e.g., [5:17-18](Job.5.17-Job.5.18); [33:15-28](Job.33.15-Job.33.28); [36:8-15](Job.36.8-Job.36.15); see [Prov 3:11](Prov.3.11); [Heb 12:2-13](Heb.12.2-Heb.12.13)); (4) part of God’s mysterious plan (e.g., [Job 11:7-8](Job.11.7-Job.11.8); [37:19](Job.37.19), [23](Job.37.23)); or (5) a test imposed on earth to satisfy a heavenly dispute (e.g., [1:6-12](Job.1.6-Job.1.12)).

Since life “under the sun” (see Ecclesiastes) is an arena too small to provide answers to all the great questions, the writer looks to the courts of heaven for a divine dimension to what takes place on earth. But the answer is not disclosed even there. Why did God entertain Satan’s challenge in the first place?

In the end, the book of Job shows God defending Job’s innocence and rejecting easy explanations of suffering. God also rejects Job’s demands for an explanation. Since Job could not possibly understand the whole universe, he should not demand an explanation of how his suffering fits into that order. The world cannot be explained in terms that humans can fully understand.

The book of Job thus offers a complex picture of God. He could have rejected Satan’s suggestion, having nothing to prove; yet he chose to allow the test, ultimately demonstrating his power and bringing defeat to Satan through the human Job. God never explains to Job what is happening behind the scenes. Instead, God challenges Job’s right to question the integrity of divine justice ([40:8](Job.40.8)).

The way to live through calamities is not just to keep a stiff upper lip but to bow reverently before God and trust his sovereign goodness. In a day of calamity, humans can respond to God by worshiping him and acknowledging the wisdom and justice of his ways, regardless of how harsh the pain or dark the confusion. God’s holy purposes for human suffering are sometimes hidden. In the end, Job draws closer to God through his suffering: “I had only heard about you before, but now I have seen you with my own eyes” ([42:5](Job.42.5)).

b.x: The opening phrase, **There once was a man***,* can introduce either a parable ([2 Sam 12:1](2Sam.12.1)) or history ([1 Sam 25:2](1Sam.25.2)).
**Job** is also mentioned in [Ezek 14:14](Ezek.14.14), [20](Ezek.14.20) and [Jas 5:11](Jas.5.11).

**Uz** is east of the Jordan, either in Edom to the south ([Gen 36:28](Gen.36.28); [1 Chr 1:42](1Chr.1.42); [Jer 25:19-20](Jer.25.19-Jer.25.20); [Lam 4:21](Lam.4.21)) or in Aram to the north ([Gen 10:23](Gen.10.23); [22:21](Gen.22.21); [1 Chr 1:17](1Chr.1.17), [42](1Chr.1.42)). Job was not an Israelite—he lived before the nation was born and outside its later territory.

Job was morally **blameless—a man of complete integrity** ([Job 1:8](Job.1.8); [2:3](Job.2.3); see [Pss 25:21](Ps.25.21); [37:37](Ps.37.37); [Prov 2:7](Prov.2.7); [20:11](Prov.20.11); [29:10](Prov.29.10)). He did not claim to be perfect or sinless ([Job 6:24](Job.6.24); [7:21](Job.7.21); see also [Eccl 7:20](Eccl.7.20); [Rom 3:23](Rom.3.23); [1 Jn 1:8](1John.1.8)), but he was righteous; his suffering did not result from guilt. He **feared God** (see [Ps 111:10](Ps.111.10); [Prov 1:7](Prov.1.7); [9:10](Prov.9.10); [2 Cor 7:1](2Cor.7.1)) and did not appeal to any of the ancient Near Eastern gods ([Job 9:8](Job.9.8); [23:13](Job.23.13); [31:26-28](Job.31.26-Job.31.28)).
Job was prosperous in **sons, daughters,** livestock, and **servants** (cp. [Gen 30:43](Gen.30.43); [Deut 7:13](Deut.7.13); [Ps 107:38](Ps.107.38)).

Numbers such as **seven** and **three** (and **7,000** and **3,000**) indicate the completeness of the blessing Job experienced (see [Job 42:13](Job.42.13); see also [Pss 127:3-5](Ps.127.3-Ps.127.5); [128:3](Ps.128.3)).

**the richest person in that entire area:** The figures that catalogue Job’s wealth might not be exact, but they are realistic for a wealthy man of that time (cp. Nabal’s wealth, [1 Sam 25:2](1Sam.25.2)).
Ritual washing and changing garments were common ways for individuals to **purify** themselves before offering a sacrifice ([Gen 35:2](Gen.35.2); [Exod 19:10](Exod.19.10), [14](Exod.19.14)).
The common time for conscientious piety was **early in the morning** (see [Gen 22:3](Gen.22.3); [Ps 5:3](Ps.5.3); [Mark 1:35](Mark.1.35)).

**cursed:** The Hebrew term *barak* (literally *blessed*) is used here as a euphemism for cursing (cp. [Job 1:11](Job.1.11); [2:5](Job.2.5), [9](Job.2.9); [1 Kgs 21:10](1Kgs.21.10), [13](1Kgs.21.13); [Ps 10:3](Ps.10.3)). Job was concerned that his children might have committed this capital crime ([Lev 24:10-16](Lev.24.10-Lev.24.16); [1 Kgs 21:9-13](1Kgs.21.9-1Kgs.21.13); cp. [Job 1:11](Job.1.11); [2:5](Job.2.5), [9](Job.2.9)). Job understood that sinful attitudes in people’s **hearts** constitute sin ([Jer 17:9-10](Jer.17.9-Jer.17.10); [Mark 7:21-23](Mark.7.21-Mark.7.23)).

God and Satan agree to a test that would bring about Job’s troubles and confirm his integrity ([1:20-21](Job.1.20-Job.1.21); [2:10](Job.2.10)). None of the book’s characters ever learn of this heavenly council.

The **members of the heavenly court** are heavenly beings; they may be either holy angels or rebellious demons ([Gen 6:2](Gen.6.2), [4](Gen.6.4)). They join God in his deliberations, including at creation ([Gen 1:26](Gen.1.26)) and in his rule over creation ([Job 1:6](Job.1.6); [Gen 3:22](Gen.3.22); [2:1](Gen.2.1); [1 Kgs 22:19-22](1Kgs.22.19-1Kgs.22.22); [Pss 82:1](Ps.82.1); [89:5](Ps.89.5), [7-8](Ps.89.7-Ps.89.8); [Dan 3:13](Dan.3.13), [17](Dan.3.17), [23](Dan.3.23), [25](Dan.3.25); [7:9-14](Dan.7.9-Dan.7.14)).
The account remains unclear as to whether **Satan** usually **came with** other members of the heavenly court to make a report or whether he was intruding as Job’s adversary.
**Where have you come from?** The question was God’s sovereign demand for a report from a subordinate (see [Gen 3:9](Gen.3.9)).

Satan was not **patrolling** to implement God’s judgments (cp. [1 Chr 21:1-14](1Chr.21.1-1Chr.21.14); [2 Kgs 19:35](2Kgs.19.35) *//* [Isa 37:36](Isa.37.36); [Ezek 1:5-9](Ezek.1.5-Ezek.1.9)) but to oppose God’s purposes ([2 Tim 2:26](2Tim.2.26); [1 Pet 5:8](1Pet.5.8)).

**my servant:** This title was used for the patriarchs ([Gen 26:24](Gen.26.24); [Exod 32:13](Exod.32.13)), the prophets ([2 Kgs 17:13](2Kgs.17.13); [Jer 7:25](Jer.7.25); [Zech 1:6](Zech.1.6)), and David (e.g., [2 Sam 7:1-29](2Sam.7.1-2Sam.7.29); [Pss 18:1](Ps.18.1); [36:1](Ps.36.1)).

**Job has good reason** (Hebrew *khinnam;* see study note on 2:3) **to fear God:** The wisdom tradition links piety with prosperity. Satan went a step further by suggesting that Job’s piety was contingent upon his affluence.

**reach out . . . test him . . . Do whatever you want:** Satan was God’s agent; the hand he put forth was the Lord’s as well as Satan’s, for here they acted against everything Job possessed and later against Job himself ([2:5-6](Job.2.5-Job.2.6)).
Job later cursed the day of his birth ([3:1](Job.3.1), [8](Job.3.8)), but he did not **curse** God ([31:30](Job.31.30)), even when his distraught wife urged him to do so ([2:9](Job.2.9)).
God allowed Satan to test Job to prove that Satan’s cynicism was incorrect ([1 Cor 10:11](1Cor.10.11); see [Jas 1:13](Jas.1.13); cp. [Luke 22:31-32](Luke.22.31-Luke.22.32); [John 19:11](John.19.11)).
These attacks destroyed the blessings enumerated in [1:2-3](Job.1.2-Job.1.3); Job was left alone with the four ominous messengers who came to report and a wife who offered misguided counsel.

The repetition of **while he was still speaking** emphasizes the relentlessness of the attacks (see [Jer 51:31](Jer.51.31)). The repetition of **I am the only one who escaped to tell you** emphasizes the total obliteration of Job’s resources.

The **Sabeans** were marauding bandit tribes from the desert (cp. [Judg 6:3](Judg.6.3)). By the 700s BC, the southern Sabeans would become a national power that traded in gold, precious stones, perfume, and slaves ([Ps 72:10](Ps.72.10); [Isa 43:3](Isa.43.3); [45:14](Isa.45.14); [60:6](Isa.60.6); [Jer 6:20](Jer.6.20)).

The **fire of God . . . from heaven** ([20:26](Job.20.26)) might have been lightning ([Lev 10:2](Lev.10.2); [1 Kgs 18:38](1Kgs.18.38); [2 Kgs 1:10-14](2Kgs.1.10-2Kgs.1.14)), wildfire ([Num 11:1-3](Num.11.1-Num.11.3)), or volcanic activity ([Gen 19:24](Gen.19.24)).
That the **wind . . . hit the house on all sides** suggests that Job and his children were settled farmers living in houses rather than nomads living in tents.

Job **tore his robe** and **shaved his head***;* both were common Near East rituals that demonstrated **grief**. These actions sometimes substituted for self-mutilation as a physical response to shock, horror, or bad news ([2:12](Job.2.12); [Gen 37:29](Gen.37.29), [34](Gen.37.34); [Judg 11:35](Judg.11.35); [Jer 16:6](Jer.16.6); [Ezek 7:18](Ezek.7.18); [Amos 8:10](Amos.8.10)).
He **fell to the ground***,* not to wail in despair, but **to worship** in hope ([1 Pet 5:6](1Pet.5.6)).
This scene is an exact repetition of the scene presented in [1:6-8](Job.1.6-Job.1.8).
The phrase **without cause** (Hebrew *khinnam*) is a wordplay on Satan’s question in [1:9](Job.1.9).
**take away his health** (literally *strike his flesh and bones*): Bones were thought to be the seat of health.
**spare** (literally *guard/watch over*): God ironically made Satan responsible for guarding Job’s **life** (cp. [10:13-14](Job.10.13-Job.10.14); [13:27](Job.13.27); [33:11](Job.33.11)).
This term for **terrible boils** was used for any inflamed, running sores ([Exod 9:10](Exod.9.10); [Lev 13:18-20](Lev.13.18-Lev.13.20); [Deut 28:27](Deut.28.27), [35](Deut.28.35)).
Job might have **scraped his skin** to relieve itching; the Greek Old Testament says that it was “to scrape away the pus.”

**The ashes** might refer to a place where lepers were quarantined, but Job was probably demonstrating his grief and dismay ([30:19](Job.30.19); [Gen 18:27](Gen.18.27); [2 Sam 13:19](2Sam.13.19); [Isa 58:5](Isa.58.5); [Jon 3:6](Jonah.3.6)).

Job’s **wife** first summarized the essence of Job’s temptation by echoing God’s words ([2:3](Job.2.3)); Job was trying to **maintain** his **integrity.** In her frustration and anguish, however, she then counseled Job to **curse God** and thus unknowingly fulfill Satan’s prediction ([1:11](Job.1.11); [2:5](Job.2.5)).

Job’s acceptance of **bad** as well as **good things** from God’s hand demonstrates his righteousness and faith (cp. [1:21](Job.1.21); [2 Sam 12:16-20](2Sam.12.16-2Sam.12.20); [Luke 22:42](Luke.22.42)).
By saying **nothing wrong***,* Job controlled his tongue ([Prov 13:3](Prov.13.3); [21:23](Prov.21.23); see [Jas 3:2](Jas.3.2)).
It might have taken several months for **Job’s friends** (see study note on 6:14-27) to hear of his afflictions (see [7:3](Job.7.3)).
The text implies that Job’s friends were Edomites, a people who were famous for their wisdom ([Jer 49:7](Jer.49.7); [Obad 1:8](Obad.1.8)).

**Eliphaz the Temanite** was probably a descendant of Esau’s grandson Teman ([Gen 36:10-11](Gen.36.10-Gen.36.11), [15](Gen.36.15)); his land was located in Edom ([Ezek 25:13](Ezek.25.13); [Amos 1:11-12](Amos.1.11-Amos.1.12)).

The *Bil-* element in **Bildad** would remind Hebrew readers of names like *Bilhan,* a descendant of Esau ([Gen 36:27](Gen.36.27); [1 Chr 1:42](1Chr.1.42)). The *-dad* element would remind them of names like *Bedad,* father of the Edomite king *Hadad* ([Gen 36:35](Gen.36.35); [1 Chr 1:46](1Chr.1.46)).
**Shuhite:** No place named Shuah is known, but Abraham’s son Shuah was sent to “a land in the east” ([Gen 25:1](Gen.25.1), [6](Gen.25.6); [1 Chr 1:32](1Chr.1.32)).

The Greek Old Testament lists **Zophar** instead of Zepho as one of Esau’s grandsons ([Gen 36:11](Gen.36.11), [15](Gen.36.15); [1 Chr 1:36](1Chr.1.36)). A **Naamathite** might reside in a town named Naamah, but no such location is known. Two Old Testament women are named Naamah, but neither is a likely ancestor of Zophar ([Gen 4:22](Gen.4.22); [1 Kgs 14:21](1Kgs.14.21)).
**they scarcely recognized him:** This expression indicates the extreme suffering Job had experienced (cp. [Isa 52:14](Isa.52.14); [53:3](Isa.53.3)).
Job’s friends mourned by **wailing loudly***,* just as they would have done for a dead man.

Throwing **dust** sometimes expressed anger or disdain (see [2 Sam 16:13](2Sam.16.13); [Acts 22:23](Acts.22.23)), but here it signaled mourning (see [Josh 7:6](Josh.7.6); [1 Sam 4:12](1Sam.4.12); [Neh 9:1](Neh.9.1); [Lam 2:10](Lam.2.10)).
Job’s friends **sat on the ground** to identify with Job’s suffering (see [2:8](Job.2.8)).

The standard period for mourning the death of a notable person or for acknowledging other disastrous news was **seven days and nights** ([Gen 50:10](Gen.50.10); [1 Sam 31:13](1Sam.31.13); see also [Ezek 3:14-15](Ezek.3.14-Ezek.3.15)).

Job’s outburst did not mean that his integrity had cracked under the strain ([42:7-8](Job.42.7-Job.42.8); [Jas 5:11](Jas.5.11)). Elijah and Jeremiah, both godly men, used the same hyperbolic language ([1 Kgs 19:4](1Kgs.19.4); [Jer 20:14-18](Jer.20.14-Jer.20.18)).
**Job spoke** and thus put at risk his refusal to sin with his mouth ([1:21](Job.1.21); [2:10](Job.2.10)).
Job **cursed the day of his birth** in great detail. However, his words sound more like pitiful complaints. Job didn’t curse God as his creator, but he lamented the conditions of his existence.

Job longed for the sinister **darkness** of the underworld ([Exod 10:22](Exod.10.22); [Prov 4:19](Prov.4.19); [Joel 2:2](Joel.2.2)) and the **gloom** of death ([Job 10:21-22](Job.10.21-Job.10.22); [38:17](Job.38.17)) to **claim** the **day** of his birth.
The expression **experts at cursing** refers to professional cursers such as Balaam ([Num 22–24](Num.22.1-Num.24.25)).
Venus and Mercury, the **morning stars***,* herald the dawn ([38:7](Job.38.7)).

**shut my mother’s womb:** Closing or opening the womb sometimes refers to conception ([Gen 16:2](Gen.16.2); [20:18](Gen.20.18); [29:31](Gen.29.31); [30:22](Gen.30.22); [1 Sam 1:5-6](1Sam.1.5-1Sam.1.6)), but here it refers to birth (see also [Job 38:8](Job.38.8)).

Job’s language turns from curse to lamentation. Job alternates between repugnance for life and a romance with death. Seven times, Job laments his situation by asking **why** ([3:11](Job.3.11), [12](Job.3.12), [16](Job.3.16), [20](Job.3.20), [23](Job.3.23); see [Pss 10:1](Ps.10.1); [22:1](Ps.22.1); [Jer 20:18](Jer.20.18); [Lam 5:20](Lam.5.20)).
The dead were thought to continue their identities and social status after death. Perhaps Job wanted **the world’s kings and prime ministers** to acknowledge his own princely status ([1:3](Job.1.3)).

**rich in gold, whose palaces were filled with silver:** This might refer to treasure-filled tombs, but it more likely refers to the futile hoarding of wealth that ends in death (as in [3:14](Job.3.14)).
Job equated **light** with **life** ([33:30](Job.33.30); see [John 1:4](John.1.4); [8:12](John.8.12)).

**Bitter** might mean “short-tempered” ([Judg 18:25](Judg.18.25)), “enraged” ([2 Sam 17:8](2Sam.17.8)), “anguish” ([Job 7:11](Job.7.11)), “distress” ([Prov 31:6](Prov.31.6)), or “discontented” ([1 Sam 1:10](1Sam.1.10); [22:2](1Sam.22.2)).
People in misery **long for death** with the desperation of those who dig for **hidden treasure**.
**Eliphaz the Temanite** (see study note on 2:11) was the most prominent and probably the oldest of Job’s friends; his speeches are longer and more ornate than the others.
**who could keep from speaking out?** Eliphaz mimicked the urgency of a prophetic revelation ([4:12-16](Job.4.12-Job.4.16); see [Jer 20:9](Jer.20.9); [Amos 3:8](Amos.3.8)).

This section begins three rounds of speeches by each of Job’s three comforters, each with a response from Job ([4:1–27:23](Job.4.1-Job.27.23)). In this first round, Job’s friends exhort him to seek God so that he can again enjoy prosperity.
**People . . . who were weak** were depressed and suffered from low morale ([Isa 13:7](Isa.13.7); [35:3](Isa.35.3); [Ezek 7:17](Ezek.7.17)).

Job probably counted his children among the **innocent** dead ([1:5](Job.1.5)), and even Eliphaz must have known that innocent blood is sometimes shed (cp. [Deut 19:10](Deut.19.10); [Prov 6:17](Prov.6.17); [Jer 7:6](Jer.7.6)).

The **harvest** metaphor illustrates the scriptural principle that behavior merits judgment ([Prov 22:8](Prov.22.8); [Hos 8:7](Hos.8.7); [Rom 2:9-11](Rom.2.9-Rom.2.11); [Gal 6:7-8](Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8)). The New Testament describes the final judgment as a harvest ([Matt 13:39](Matt.13.39)). Jesus rejected simplistic attempts to analyze people’s lives by this principle ([Luke 13:4](Luke.13.4); [John 9:1-3](John.9.1-John.9.3)).
**They vanish in a blast of his anger:** Eliphaz understood the wind of [1:19](Job.1.19) as divine judgment (cp. [Isa 40:7](Isa.40.7); [Hos 13:15](Hos.13.15)).
Eliphaz posed as a prophet, implying that God spoke to him **in secret** ([Num 12:6](Num.12.6)); later God did speak to him, but not to affirm his counsel ([Job 42:7](Job.42.7)).
Eliphaz probably referred to the God-induced **sleep** associated with prophetic vision ([33:15](Job.33.15); [Gen 15:12](Gen.15.12); [Num 12:6](Num.12.6); [Isa 29:10](Isa.29.10)).

**Fear** is common in God’s presence ([Gen 15:12](Gen.15.12); [Dan 8:17-18](Dan.8.17-Dan.8.18); [10:8-10](Dan.10.8-Dan.10.10)), but God tells his people not to be afraid ([Gen 15:1](Gen.15.1); [26:24](Gen.26.24); [Isa 40:9](Isa.40.9); [44:8](Isa.44.8)).
Eliphaz’s **bones trembled** like those of a prophet with terrible news to deliver ([Jer 23:9](Jer.23.9); [Hab 3:16](Hab.3.16)).
**A spirit** (or *wind*) **swept past my face:** Wind is a physical display of God’s powerful presence ([38:1](Job.38.1); [Nah 1:3](Nah.1.3); [Acts 2:2](Acts.2.2); cp. [1 Kgs 19:11](1Kgs.19.11)).

As the characters in the book repeatedly acknowledge, no one is truly **innocent** or **pure** (see [9:2](Job.9.2); [15:14](Job.15.14); [25:4](Job.25.4); [35:7](Job.35.7)) because all are depraved ([Pss 14:3](Ps.14.3); [53:3](Ps.53.3); [Rom 3:10-11](Rom.3.10-Rom.3.11)). Eliphaz used these terms to mean that human beings are sinful creatures and God is the sinless Creator. Job and God used them to mean that Job had faithfully carried out the duties inherent in his relationship with God. Job and Eliphaz never agreed on the meaning of these terms. Later, God said that Eliphaz had spoken inaccurately ([Job 42:7](Job.42.7)).
The concept that **God does not trust his own angels** and that he **charged his messengers with foolishness** is otherwise unknown (but see [Gen 6:1-4](Gen.6.1-Gen.6.4)).
A **tent** was a common symbol for mortal life ([Isa 38:12](Isa.38.12); [2 Cor 5:1](2Cor.5.1); cp. [Eccl 12:6](Eccl.12.6)).

**The angels** (literally *the holy ones*), probably a reference back to [4:18](Job.4.18), are called “holy ones” because of their proximity to God, not because they were morally perfect ([15:15](Job.15.15); [Dan 4:14](Dan.4.14); [8:13](Dan.8.13); [Zech 14:5](Zech.14.5)).

The **court** (literally *the gate*) was the site of legal and commercial deliberations in which Job had participated ([29:7](Job.29.7); see [Deut 21:19-21](Deut.21.19-Deut.21.21); [Ruth 4:1-11](Ruth.4.1-Ruth.4.11)).

To **go to God** meant lodging a formal appeal with God for assistance, counsel, or vindication, sometimes by way of repentance ([Amos 5:4](Amos.5.4), [6](Amos.5.6)) and possibly through a prophetic oracle ([Gen 25:22](Gen.25.22); [1 Sam 9:9](1Sam.9.9); [1 Kgs 22:8](1Kgs.22.8)).

Job wanted to **present** his **case** to God ([Job 13:3](Job.13.3), [15](Job.13.15), [18](Job.13.18); [23:3-8](Job.23.3-Job.23.8)), and later he attempted to do so ([29:1–31:40](Job.29.1-Job.31.40)).

Eliphaz’s doxology praised God as the wonder-working Creator and Sustainer of the universe ([5:9-10](Job.5.9-Job.5.10)) and as the righteous Judge who brings down the powerful and lifts up the poor ([5:11-16](Job.5.11-Job.5.16)).
Job’s region depended upon **rain** rather than irrigation (see [36:27-28](Job.36.27-Job.36.28)).
God **traps the wise** in the cleverness of their words ([Prov 12:13](Prov.12.13)). Paul alluded to this verse in his rejection of worldly wisdom ([1 Cor 1:19](1Cor.1.19)).
**the discipline of the Almighty:** See [Deut 8:5](Deut.8.5); [Prov 3:11-12](Prov.3.11-Prov.3.12); [Rev 3:19](Rev.3.19).
**six disasters . . . even in the seventh:** This wisdom formula reflects a sense of completeness (cp. [Prov 30:15-31](Prov.30.15-Prov.30.31)).

This list reflects Mosaic covenant blessings and curses ([Lev 26](Lev.26.1-Lev.26.46); [Deut 28](Deut.28.1-Deut.28.68)). Eliphaz thought that people in right relationship with God would be free from **famine** ([Job 5:20](Job.5.20), [22](Job.5.22); see [Lev 26:4-5](Lev.26.4-Lev.26.5), [10](Lev.26.10); [Deut 28:4-6](Deut.28.4-Deut.28.6), [8](Deut.28.8), [11-12](Deut.28.11-Deut.28.12)), **war** (i.e., death, [Job 5:20](Job.5.20)) and the **destruction** it causes ([5:21](Job.5.21), [22](Job.5.22); see [Lev 26:6-8](Lev.26.6-Lev.26.8); [Deut 28:7](Deut.28.7), [48](Deut.28.48)), and **slander**. They will even be **at peace** with **wild animals** ([Job 5:23](Job.5.23); see [Lev 26:6](Lev.26.6)) and **the stones of the field**. This peace might indicate fertile rather than stony fields ([2 Kgs 3:19](2Kgs.3.19), [25](2Kgs.3.25); [Matt 13:5](Matt.13.5)), or it might symbolize wider harmony with the natural world (see [Ps 91:11-12](Ps.91.11-Ps.91.12)).
**nothing will be missing:** See [Deut 28:11-12](Deut.28.11-Deut.28.12); cp. [Job 1:6-19](Job.1.6-Job.1.19).
**descendants . . . as plentiful as grass:** See [Gen 22:17](Gen.22.17); [Lev 26:9](Lev.26.9); [Deut 28:4](Deut.28.4), [11-12](Deut.28.11-Deut.28.12).

Job’s response attacks his counselors (ch [6](Job.6.1-Job.6.30)) and challenges God (ch [7](Job.7.1-Job.7.21)). He excuses his passionate words by referencing the depths of his misery ([6:2-3](Job.6.2-Job.6.3); [7:11](Job.7.11)). Job says that Eliphaz has failed to offer comfort or sympathy as a friend, having chosen instead to haggle over stale theological precepts.

In the Old Testament, **arrows** are associated with supernatural peril, pestilence, and destructive ills ([7:20](Job.7.20); [16:12-13](Job.16.12-Job.16.13); [Deut 32:23-24](Deut.32.23-Deut.32.24), [42](Deut.32.42); [Pss 7:12-13](Ps.7.12-Ps.7.13); [38:2](Ps.38.2); [64:7](Ps.64.7); [91:5-6](Ps.91.5-Ps.91.6); [Lam 2:4](Lam.2.4); [3:12-13](Lam.3.12-Lam.3.13); [Ezek 5:16](Ezek.5.16)).
**the tasteless white of an egg?** Job’s riddle-like complaint probably refers both to Eliphaz’s weak counsel and the detestable situation God had allowed him to endure.
At one time, both Moses and Elijah wished that God would **kill** them ([Num 11:15](Num.11.15); [1 Kgs 19:4](1Kgs.19.4)).

Job and his friends might have been bound by a covenant of loyalty and faithfulness (Hebrew *khesed;* see [Gen 21:23](Gen.21.23); [Exod 15:13](Exod.15.13); [1 Chr 16:34](1Chr.16.34)) that made them like brothers ([Job 6:14-15](Job.6.14-Job.6.15)), protectors ([6:21-23](Job.6.21-Job.6.23)), and trusted friends ([6:27](Job.6.27)). If this was the case, Job was accusing his friends of violating their covenant with him.

The city of **Tema** in the northern Arabian desert was at the junction of roads from Damascus to Mecca and from the Persian Gulf to Aqaba ([Isa 21:14](Isa.21.14); [Jer 25:23](Jer.25.23)). It might have been named after one of Ishmael’s descendants ([Gen 25:15](Gen.25.15)). It was not the same as Teman, Eliphaz’s home in Edom.

**Sheba,** located in southwest Arabia, was a market city for precious commodities ([Ps 72:10](Ps.72.10), [15](Ps.72.15); [Isa 60:6](Isa.60.6); [Jer 6:20](Jer.6.20); [Ezek 27:22-23](Ezek.27.22-Ezek.27.23); [38:13](Ezek.38.13)).

**even send an orphan into slavery:** Job, the former protector of orphans ([31:17](Job.31.17), [21](Job.31.21)), used a proverbial example of his counselors’ hard-heartedness toward the defenseless (see [17:5](Job.17.5)).

**Don’t I know the difference between right and wrong?** (literally *Can’t my palate discern malice?*): Job might have been echoing his earlier comment about a tasteless, revolting diet ([6:6-7](Job.6.6-Job.6.7)).

A **worker** was **to be paid** at the end of each day ([Lev 19:13](Lev.19.13); [Deut 24:15](Deut.24.15)), though this did not always happen ([Jer 22:13](Jer.22.13); [Mal 3:5](Mal.3.5); [Jas 5:4](Jas.5.4)).
Job’s trial might already have gone on for **months.**

The Hebrew term (*‘amal*) that runs throughout Job is translated as “**misery**/miserable” ([3:20](Job.3.20); [11:16](Job.11.16); [16:2](Job.16.2); [20:22](Job.20.22)) or as “trouble” ([3:10](Job.3.10); [4:8](Job.4.8); [5:6](Job.5.6), [7](Job.5.7); [15:35](Job.15.35)).
Job’s reference to **maggots** signified mortality ([25:6](Job.25.6)) and the rampant corruption of Sheol ([17:14](Job.17.14); [21:26](Job.21.26); [24:20](Job.24.20); see [Isa 14:11](Isa.14.11)).
Job cried out to God, complaining that life was too brief ([7:6-10](Job.7.6-Job.7.10)). This complaint contrasts ironically with his earlier desire that God end it all ([6:9](Job.6.9)).
Those who call upon **God** to **remember** are typically seeking covenant mercy ([Pss 35:6](Ps.35.6); [106:4](Ps.106.4)).
Job’s declaration that **life is but a breath** (Hebrew *ruakh*) meant either that he was one breath away from death or that his life was like a passing wind ([Ps 39:9](Ps.39.9), [11](Ps.39.11)).
**You see me now, but not for long:** The Greek Old Testament omitted this verse to avoid the implication that God would be unable to see Job in Sheol (see study note on 7:9).

**die** (literally *go down to Sheol*): This is the first explicit mention of Sheol in Job. It is described as a place of rest from earthly pressures and distinctions ([3:13-19](Job.3.13-Job.3.19)) and as a dark dwelling place ([10:21-22](Job.10.21-Job.10.22); [17:13](Job.17.13)) deep in the earth ([11:8](Job.11.8)) that is covered in dust ([17:16](Job.17.16)). It is the destiny of all the living ([30:23](Job.30.23)) from which no one can return ([10:21](Job.10.21); see [Gen 37:25](Gen.37.25); [2 Sam 12:12](2Sam.12.12)).
**I cannot keep from speaking:** Job echoed Eliphaz’s inability to refrain from words ([4:2](Job.4.2)).

The **sea monster** (Hebrew *yam*) and **dragon** (Hebrew *tannin*) represent chaotic opposition to God’s orderly creation. In Canaanite mythology, Yam was the primordial sea god and Tannin was a sea monster ([Jer 51:34](Jer.51.34)) or a mythological deity of chaos ([Ps 74:13-14](Ps.74.13-Ps.74.14)). This kind of chaos is also represented in Job as *Leviathan* ([Job 3:8](Job.3.8); [Isa 27:1](Isa.27.1)) or *Rahab* ([Job 9:13](Job.9.13); [26:12](Job.26.12); [Isa 51:9](Isa.51.9)). The Lord is sovereign over the sea and all that it represents ([Job 26:12](Job.26.12); [38:8-11](Job.38.8-Job.38.11); [Ps 89:9-10](Ps.89.9-Ps.89.10); [Jer 5:22](Jer.5.22)).
Job’s sickbed **dreams** and **visions** echoed those of Eliphaz ([4:12-16](Job.4.12-Job.4.16)).
**for my few remaining days:** Literally *for my days are a vapor* (Hebrew *hebel*); see “[All Is ‘Vapor’](themes:AllIsVapor)” Theme Note.
**that you should make so much of us:** Cp. [Ps 8:4-5](Ps.8.4-Ps.8.5), which treats the same thoughts positively.
**examine** (Hebrew *paqad*): In [Ps 8:4](Ps.8.4), the same term means “to honor or care for”; Job used the term ironically, meaning “to be pestered” (cp. “attacked,” [Isa 26:14](Isa.26.14)).

**Won’t you leave me alone** (literally *How long will you not look away from me*): Job sought the opposite of the watchful care that faithful people usually seek ([Num 6:25](Num.6.25); [Pss 27:9](Ps.27.9); [69:17](Ps.69.17); [80:3](Ps.80.3), [7](Ps.80.7), [19](Ps.80.19); [Lam 1:9](Lam.1.9)).
**to swallow:** This is equivalent to “a chance to catch my breath.”

**watcher of all humanity:** Rather than praising God for his goodness expressed in watchfulness ([Deut 32:10](Deut.32.10); [Ps 25:21](Ps.25.21); [Prov 24:12](Prov.24.12)), Job blamed God for hostile surveillance, which actually characterizes Satan’s activity ([Job 1:7](Job.1.7)).
**Why** is from the language of lament (see study note on 3:11-24).
**your target:** See [6:4](Job.6.4); [Lam 3:12](Lam.3.12).

Like Eliphaz, **Bildad the Shuhite** (see study note on 2:11) believed that Job’s sufferings were God’s retribution ([8:3-6](Job.8.3-Job.8.6), [13](Job.8.13); cp. [4:7-8](Job.4.7-Job.4.8); [5:2-3](Job.5.2-Job.5.3)). This counselor revered the wisdom of the past ([8:8-10](Job.8.8-Job.8.10); cp. [4:7](Job.4.7)) and addressed Job with a mixture of instruction ([8:3-6](Job.8.3-Job.8.6), [8-10](Job.8.8-Job.8.10); cp. [4:12-21](Job.4.12-Job.4.21); [5:9-16](Job.5.9-Job.5.16)) and encouragement ([8:5-7](Job.8.5-Job.8.7), [20-22](Job.8.20-Job.8.22); cp. [4:6](Job.4.6); [5:19-26](Job.5.19-Job.5.26)). His point was that Job should quit blustering. He advised Job to repent and allow God’s justice to bring about restoration ([8:1-7](Job.8.1-Job.8.7)).
**How long?** Bildad’s question might be an ironic parody of Job’s question in [7:19](Job.7.19).

According to Bildad, **God** does not **twist justice***,* so the death of Job’s children proved that they had **sinned against** God. Bildad divided people into the blameless (Hebrew *tam,* [8:20a](Job.8.20); see [1:1](Job.1.1)) and the secretly wicked (Hebrew *khanep,* [8:13b](Job.8.13)). He believed that they could be differentiated by watching what God did to them.
**you will end with much:** Bildad’s words were more true than he realized ([42:12](Job.42.12); cp. [5:19-26](Job.5.19-Job.5.26)).
Bildad made the case for traditional wisdom by appealing to ancient tradition and history ([Deut 4:32](Deut.4.32); [Jer 18:13](Jer.18.13)).
**born but yesterday and know nothing:** Bildad suggested that Job’s generation was either born too late to be acquainted with ancient wisdom or was too young to have accumulated it.
**Papyrus reeds grow** as high as ten to fifteen feet.

To **forget God** does not mean to have a lapse of memory but to act as if God did not exist (see [Pss 10:4](Ps.10.4); [14:1](Ps.14.1); [Zeph 1:12](Zeph.1.12)) or cannot see (see [Job 22:13-17](Job.22.13-Job.22.17); [Ps 94:7](Ps.94.7)).
In this parable, a **plant** with **roots** that **grow down through a pile of stones** gains stability by becoming entwined with the rocks.

Job responded to Bildad by describing God’s cosmic and judicial power. His speech sounds like a complicated legal case, with a summons and response ([9:3](Job.9.3), [14-16](Job.9.14-Job.9.16), [19b](Job.9.19), [32](Job.9.32)), the possibility of self-incrimination ([9:20](Job.9.20)), an arbiter ([9:33-34](Job.9.33-Job.9.34)), an accusatory question ([9:12](Job.9.12)), a legal sentence ([9:22](Job.9.22)), and a declaration of guilt ([9:28-30](Job.9.28-Job.9.30)).
**If someone wanted to take God to court:** Job later expressed the wish to meet God in court ([13:3](Job.13.3), [15](Job.13.15), [23](Job.13.23); [23:4](Job.23.4)).

When God **moves the mountains** and when the **foundations** of the earth **tremble**, it is a sign of his presence as lawgiver ([Exod 19:18](Exod.19.18)), judge ([Jer 4:24](Jer.4.24)), or rescuer ([Ps 18:7](Ps.18.7); [Isa 13:13](Isa.13.13); [29:6](Isa.29.6)).
The **Bear** (also at [38:32](Job.38.32)) is commonly identified as Arcturus but might also refer to the constellations of Ursa Minor or Leo.
The **Pleiades** is a group of seven stars ([38:31](Job.38.31); [Amos 5:8](Amos.5.8)).

**monsters of the sea** (literally *the helpers of Rahab*): Job personified demonic powers as creatures like this mythical sea monster that represents chaos in ancient literature ([26:12](Job.26.12); [Ps 89:11](Ps.89.11); [Isa 51:9](Isa.51.9)).

**with a storm:** Perhaps the words translated “with a storm” (*bis’arah)* are a double entendre with *besa‘arah* (“for a hair”; i.e., “for the littlest thing”), which would parallel **without cause.**

Job was indeed **innocent** ([1:1](Job.1.1), [7](Job.1.7); [2:3](Job.2.3)), and he maintained this claim throughout the debate ([23:11-12](Job.23.11-Job.23.12); [27:5](Job.27.5); [31:1-40](Job.31.1-Job.31.40)).
The word **you** makes it clear that this is a prayer, although the phrase **O God** is not explicit in the Hebrew.
**wash myself:** Job spoke of cleansing himself with the strongest **soap** to represent ridding himself of all sin ([1:5](Job.1.5); cp. [Ps 26:6](Ps.26.6); [Matt 27:24](Matt.27.24)).
The **muddy ditch** (literally *pit*) can refer to the place of the dead ([17:14](Job.17.14); [33:18](Job.33.18)), so it might allude to the defilement of death.
The **filthy clothing** of guilt contrasts with the clean clothes of acquittal ([Zech 3:3-5](Zech.3.3-Zech.3.5); see [Isa 61:10](Isa.61.10); [64:6](Isa.64.6); [Rev 19:8](Rev.19.8)).
A **mediator** would not judge God and man but would work to **bring** them **together** (see [16:19-21](Job.16.19-Job.16.21)).
A succession of images describes God’s role in creating Job.

**You formed me with your hands . . . made me from dust:** This was how a potter made a vessel ([Isa 45:9](Isa.45.9); [Jer 18:1-12](Jer.18.1-Jer.18.12)). Although the potter has incontestable sovereignty over the clay ([Isa 45:9](Isa.45.9); [Jer 18:5-12](Jer.18.5-Jer.18.12); [Rom 9:20-25](Rom.9.20-Rom.9.25)), Job was questioning God.

**back to dust:** This common motif in Job represents the temporary nature of life ([Job 4:19](Job.4.19); [7:9-10](Job.7.9-Job.7.10), [21](Job.7.21); [14:1-2](Job.14.1-Job.14.2), [10](Job.14.10); see [Gen 3:19](Gen.3.19)).

**You guided my conception and formed me in the womb:** The Hebrew terminology (literally *You poured me out like milk and curdled me like cheese*) evokes graphic images of a newborn baby still covered with the creamy substance called vernix.

Earlier, Job had painted a fairly pleasant picture of Sheol ([3:13-19](Job.3.13-Job.3.19)); now he describes it as a **land of darkness and utter gloom** (see also [7:9-10](Job.7.9-Job.7.10); [14:7-22](Job.14.7-Job.14.22)).
**Zophar the Naamathite** (see study note on 2:11), the most severe of Job’s three friends, dealt only with the issue of sin.
**this torrent of words:** Verbosity is characteristic of fools ([Prov 10:8](Prov.10.8), [14](Job.10.14)) and sinners ([Prov 10:19](Prov.10.19)), but Job was innocent.
**mock God:** Zophar viewed Job’s words about God’s justice as sinfully sarcastic ([Job 10:2-7](Job.10.2-Job.10.7), [13-15](Job.10.13-Job.10.15)).
**My beliefs are pure:** Job was not defining doctrine but defending his own integrity.
**punishing you . . . less than you deserve:** Zophar believed that calamity indicated divine retribution for sins (cp. [34:36](Job.34.36)).

No one can **discover everything about the Almighty** (literally *find out the limits of the Almighty*), who is beyond the limits of the heavens, underworld, land, and sea ([11:8-9](Job.11.8-Job.11.9)).

Zophar laid out three conditions for restoration ([11:15](Job.11.15)): (1) **prepare your heart***,* in an inward act that is not just a ritual; (2) **lift up your hands***,* a symbolic gesture of prayer, appeal ([Exod 9:29](Exod.9.29); [Prov 1:24](Prov.1.24); [Isa 1:15](Isa.1.15)), or surrender; (3) **leave all iniquity***,* not by sacrifice and remorse, but by quitting the sin (cp. [Heb 11:6](Heb.11.6); [Jas 4:8](Jas.4.8); [5:16](Jas.5.16)).
In his longest speech thus far, Job addresses not only Zophar’s remarks but the entire first round of speeches.
A switch from *you* (plural in [12:2-3](Job.12.2-Job.12.3)) to **you** (singular here) probably indicates that Job is directing his comments to Zophar.

**ask the animals . . . birds . . . earth . . . fish:** Job believed that the reason for his misery was obvious and that even nature would understand it ([Prov 6:6](Prov.6.6)). Later, God directed Job’s attention to the animal kingdom to convince Job that he did not understand ([Job 38–40](Job.38.1-Job.40.24)).

**from the hand of the** **LORD:** This is the only place in the dialogues (chs [3–27](Job.3.1-Job.27.23); [29–37](Job.29.1-Job.37.24)) that the Hebrew *Yahweh* (“the LORD”) is used. For Job, the dispute was not about who caused his misery but why it happened.
**the mouth distinguishes between foods:** See [6:6-7](Job.6.6-Job.6.7).
**Wisdom belongs to the aged:** Job’s friends defended this opinion ([8:8-10](Job.8.8-Job.8.10); [15:10](Job.15.10); [32:6-9](Job.32.6-Job.32.9)), but Job questioned it ([12:20](Job.12.20)).

**stripped of good judgment:** The NLT adds “of good judgment” for clarity. In this image, God metaphorically strips leaders of their abilities. It could also refer to being stripped of the symbols of office or to becoming naked captives ([12:18-19](Job.12.18-Job.12.19)).

When God **removes the royal robe of kings***,* he takes away the symbols of their authority (cp. [19:9](Job.19.9)). It could also be translated as “God loosens the bonds of kings,” referring to the bondage they have imposed on others.
The **priests** are figuratively **stripped of status** (the NLT adds “of status” for clarity) or are actually stripped of priestly robes; they might even be naked captives ([12:18](Job.12.18)).
**pours disgrace upon princes:** Cp. [Ps 107:40](Ps.107.40).
**disarms** (literally *looses the belt of*): The **strong** are no longer girded for battle.
**uncovers mysteries** (literally *uncovers the deeps*): This phrase might allude to Zophar’s words that God’s knowledge is “deeper than the underworld” ([11:8](Job.11.8)).

**darkness . . . deepest gloom:** The Old Testament often describes God as dwelling in darkness ([1 Kgs 8:12](1Kgs.8.12); [2 Chr 6:1](2Chr.6.1)) and as manifesting himself through darkness ([2 Sam 22:10](2Sam.22.10), [12](2Sam.22.12); [Ps 18:9](Ps.18.9), [11](Ps.18.11)), as when he gave the law at Sinai ([Deut 4:11](Deut.4.11); [5:22-23](Deut.5.22-Deut.5.23)) or when he comes in judgment ([Zeph 1:15](Zeph.1.15)).
**strips kings of understanding:** See [Job 12:18](Job.12.18); cp. [Dan 4:23](Dan.4.23), [32-33](Dan.4.32-Dan.4.33).
**He . . . leaves them wandering in a pathless wasteland** like the princes in [Ps 107:40](Ps.107.40) (see [Job 12:21](Job.12.21)).

Perhaps foolish counsel made the kings **stagger like drunkards** ([12:17](Job.12.17); see [Isa 19:14](Isa.19.14)); it resulted from “drinking” God’s wrath ([Ps 75:8](Ps.75.8); [Jer 25:15-27](Jer.25.15-Jer.25.27)).
Job appealed to experience, as his comforters had done ([3:12-17](Job.3.12-Job.3.17); [5:2](Job.5.2)).
**defending God with lies:** False witnesses were forbidden even if speaking on God’s behalf ([Exod 20:16](Exod.20.16)).
**Ashes** are worthless (cp. [Isa 44:20](Isa.44.20)).
Job had contemplated finding an arbiter to **remove** God’s **heavy hand** ([9:33-34](Job.9.33-Job.9.34)). Eliphaz had urged Job to accept God’s chastening ([5:17](Job.5.17)).

Job wanted God to **summon** him, and then Job would **answer** in his own defense; or Job would **speak to** God, and then God would **reply** to substantiate the charges against Job. Since God did not take the first option, Job initiated the second one ([13:23](Job.13.23)). Eventually, God did summon Job ([38:1-3](Job.38.1-Job.38.3); [40:1-2](Job.40.1-Job.40.2)), and Job was unable to reply ([40:3-5](Job.40.3-Job.40.5)).
God can **turn away** in wrath ([Deut 31:18](Deut.31.18); [Isa 54:8](Isa.54.8); [Jer 33:5](Jer.33.5)) or refuse to show friendship ([Pss 30:7](Ps.30.7); [69:17](Ps.69.17); [102:2](Ps.102.2)).
Job, perhaps playing on his own name (*’iyyob*), denied that he was God’s **enemy** (*’oyeb*).

In the Old Testament, **dry straw** is a common image for what can be blown away (“chaff,” [Ps 83:13](Ps.83.13); [Isa 40:24](Isa.40.24); [Jer 13:24](Jer.13.24)) or burned ([Exod 15:7](Exod.15.7); [Isa 47:14](Isa.47.14); [Mal 4:1](Mal.4.1); see also “dry grass,” [Isa 5:24](Isa.5.24); [33:11](Isa.33.11)), or for what is weak ([Job 41:20-21](Job.41.20-Job.41.21)) and trifling ([Isa 41:2](Isa.41.2)).
A **shadow** passes swiftly ([1 Chr 29:15](1Chr.29.15); [Ps 102:11](Ps.102.11)).
**keep an eye on:** Job lamented God’s relentless surveillance ([7:8](Job.7.8), [17-20](Job.7.17-Job.7.20); [10:6](Job.10.6), [14](Job.10.14); [13:27](Job.13.27)).

**do not rise again:** Job himself did not have even the minimal evidence of resurrection found in the Old Testament ([2 Kgs 13:21](2Kgs.13.21); [Isa 26:19](Isa.26.19); [Dan 12:2](Dan.12.2); cp. [Job 19:25](Job.19.25)).

Job was not focusing on the end of the universe when **the heavens** will be **no more** ([Ps 102:25-26](Ps.102.25-Ps.102.26); [Isa 34:4](Isa.34.4); [51:6](Isa.51.6); [Heb 1:10-12](Heb.1.10-Heb.1.12)) but on the eternity of the heavens ([Ps 148:6](Ps.148.6); cp. [Pss 72:5](Ps.72.5), [7](Ps.72.7), [17](Ps.72.17); [89:29](Ps.89.29), [37](Ps.89.37)). His phrase refers to the permanency of death.

Since the grave is a permanent abode ([14:10-12](Job.14.10-Job.14.12), see [3:13-19](Job.3.13-Job.3.19); [7:6-10](Job.7.6-Job.7.10); [10:20-22](Job.10.20-Job.10.22)), Job could not even fulfill his request from [13:20-21](Job.13.20-Job.13.21) by hiding temporarily **in the grave.**
**guard my steps:** Here, Job refers to God’s providential care ([10:12](Job.10.12)) rather than to his surveillance ([13:27](Job.13.27); [14:3](Job.14.3)).
If **sins** are **sealed in a pouch** they do not await a time of reckoning ([Deut 32:34-35](Deut.32.34-Deut.32.35); [Hos 13:12](Hos.13.12))—they are hidden forever. Job was requesting acquittal.

Job no longer saw Sheol as a haven ([3:17-19](Job.3.17-Job.3.19); [14:13-17](Job.14.13-Job.14.17)). The Old Testament usually depicts the dead as being without feeling ([Ps 88:12](Ps.88.12); [Eccl 9:5](Eccl.9.5); cp. [Isa 50:11](Isa.50.11); [66:24](Isa.66.24)); the doctrine that the dead **suffer painfully** is clearer in the New Testament ([Luke 16:23](Luke.16.23), [28](Luke.16.28); [Rev 14:11](Rev.14.11)).
In this second round of speeches, Job’s friends focus on the fate of the wicked and imply that Job’s condition shows he has sinned.

**You are nothing but a windbag** (literally *You fill your belly with the east wind*): Since the east wind was hot, it might represent heated ([Exod 14:21](Exod.14.21); [Hos 13:15](Hos.13.15); [Jon 4:8](Jonah.4.8)) or violent ([Job 27:21](Job.27.21); [Jer 18:17](Jer.18.17)) speech.
**Your own mouth condemns you:** Job feared that this would happen ([9:20](Job.9.20); see [Matt 26:65](Matt.26.65)).
When the Lord himself later issued a similar challenge, Job found it convicting ([38:1-11](Job.38.1-Job.38.11)).

The book’s readers know about **God’s secret council** ([1:6-12](Job.1.6-Job.1.12); [2:1-6](Job.2.1-Job.2.6); see [1 Kgs 22:19-20](1Kgs.22.19-1Kgs.22.20); [Ps 89:5-7](Ps.89.5-Ps.89.7)), but Job and his company did not.
**Aged, gray-haired men** claim a monopoly on wisdom ([8:8-10](Job.8.8-Job.8.10); [12:20](Job.12.20); see [12:2](Job.12.2)).
**What has weakened your vision** (literally *Why do your eyes blink*): This sentence might be a metaphor for unbelief, or it could indicate winking like a schemer or blinking in disbelief.
**Can any mortal be pure?** Eliphaz repeated himself ([4:17-19](Job.4.17-Job.4.19)) and Job ([7:17](Job.7.17); [14:4](Job.14.4)).
**anyone born of a woman:** Both “mortal” and “born of woman” imply weakness.
The **heavens***,* traditionally associated with purity ([Exod 24:10](Exod.24.10)), were **not absolutely pure;** they had been defiled, perhaps by rebellious angels ([Job 1:6-7](Job.1.6-Job.1.7)).
**before any foreigners arrived:** Eliphaz’s contempt for foreign ideas is ironic because wisdom literature has a more international flavor than is characteristic of other Old Testament writings.

**The wicked** also suffer everything that happened to Job (see [1:16-19](Job.1.16-Job.1.19))—attacks by marauders ([15:21](Job.15.21)), loss of possessions ([15:29](Job.15.29)), crumbled houses ([15:28](Job.15.28)), and fire ([15:30](Job.15.30), [34](Job.15.34)).

Although Eliphaz generalized the **terror** that the wicked experience, Job had undergone similar experiences ([3:25](Job.3.25); [6:4](Job.6.4); [9:34](Job.9.34); [13:11](Job.13.11), [21](Job.13.21); [23:15](Job.23.15); [27:20](Job.27.20); [30:15](Job.30.15)). Bildad ([18:11](Job.18.11), [14](Job.18.14)) and Zophar ([20:25](Job.20.25)) spoke of more terror to come.

The Sabeans and Chaldeans were examples of **the destroyer** ([1:13-17](Job.1.13-Job.1.17)), but this could refer to any destructive agent ([1:18-19](Job.1.18-Job.1.19)). Destroyers might be agents of Satan ([1 Cor 10:10](1Cor.10.10); [Rev 9:11](Rev.9.11)) or divine agents that punish wickedness ([Exod 12:23](Exod.12.23); [2 Sam 24:16](2Sam.24.16); [2 Chr 32:21](2Chr.32.21); [Acts 12:23](Acts.12.23); [Heb 11:28](Heb.11.28)). Eliphaz meant the latter.
**for fear they will be murdered** (literally *he is marked for the sword*): The wicked might be killed by murder or by the sword of God’s wrath.

**They wander around, saying, “Where can I find bread?”:** Like the wicked ([15:20](Job.15.20)), Job either experienced hunger (see [15:27](Job.15.27)) or (following the Greek Old Testament) had been “appointed to be food for a vulture,” which would parallel “marked for the sword” ([15:22](Job.15.22)).
Job had complained earlier that God was treating him like a formidable foe ([7:19-21](Job.7.19-Job.7.21); [13:24](Job.13.24)).

**The burning sun** (literally *The flame*) might be the scorching sun or a flame of judgment from God ([15:34](Job.15.34), see [Num 16:31-35](Num.16.31-Num.16.35); [Ps 106:17-18](Ps.106.17-Ps.106.18); [Ezek 20:47](Ezek.20.47)).
The **breath of God** might be a desert wind or a more direct theophany (a manifestation of God’s presence) that caused the burning of [Job 15:34](Job.15.34).
The flame of judgment ([15:30](Job.15.30)) will **burn** the unjust gain of the **godless.**

Job might have wanted to **shake** his **head** in mockery or in horror ([2 Kgs 19:21](2Kgs.19.21); [Pss 22:7](Ps.22.7); [109:25](Ps.109.25); [Isa 37:22](Isa.37.22); [Jer 18:16](Jer.18.16); [Lam 2:15](Lam.2.15); [Matt 27:39](Matt.27.39)).
Job’s **family** here means his extended household, including his servants ([1:15-19](Job.1.15-Job.1.19)).
**jeer and laugh at me:** Job was the subject of mockery (cp. [Ps 35:21](Ps.35.21); [Isa 57:4](Isa.57.4); [Lam 2:16](Lam.2.16); [3:46](Lam.3.46)).

To **slap** the **cheek** was less an act of violence ([Ps 3:7](Ps.3.7); [Mic 5:1](Mic.5.1)) than an insult ([1 Kgs 22:24](1Kgs.22.24); [Isa 50:6](Isa.50.6); [Lam 3:30](Lam.3.30); [Matt 26:67](Matt.26.67)).

**took me by the neck:** This might refer to a wild animal with its prey (see [16:9](Job.16.9)), but it is more likely a military image that signaled defeat ([Gen 49:8](Gen.49.8); [Ps 18:40](Ps.18.40)).
**pierce me:** Literally *pierce my kidneys.*
**my blood:** Literally *my gall*. The picture is of wounds to vital organs.

**Again and again he smashes against me:** Job pictures himself as a fortress that God is besieging. Job saw God as a **warrior** (cp. [Exod 15:3](Exod.15.3); [Ps 24:8](Ps.24.8)) who did not defend him or offer him salvation ([Jer 20:11](Jer.20.11); [Zeph 3:17](Zeph.3.17)) but attacked him as though he were dangerous ([Job 6:12](Job.6.12); see [Isa 42:13](Isa.42.13)).

Since Job insisted on his innocence, his wearing **burlap** (literally *I sewed on burlap*) was a sign of mourning, not penitence. Perhaps it was attached to indicate that he would never remove it because he could never be consoled ([Gen 37:34-35](Gen.37.34-Gen.37.35)).

**My pride lies in the dust** (literally *I have buried my horn in the dust*): A horn symbolized dignity and power ([1 Sam 2:1](1Sam.2.1); [Pss 75:4-5](Ps.75.4-Ps.75.5); [89:17](Ps.89.17), [24](Ps.89.24); [92:10](Ps.92.10); [112:9](Ps.112.9); [148:14](Ps.148.14)); cutting it off inflicted degrading humiliation ([Ps 75:10](Ps.75.10); [Jer 48:25](Jer.48.25); [Zech 1:12](Zech.1.12)).

**done no wrong** (or *done no violence;* Hebrew *lo’-khamas*): If *violence* is the meaning, Job was possibly denying that he was a formidable warrior who should be attacked ([16:12-14](Job.16.12-Job.16.14); see also [Isa 59:6](Isa.59.6); [Jon 3:8](Jonah.3.8)).

Contrary to Eliphaz’s charge ([Job 15:4-5](Job.15.4-Job.15.5)) and Bildad’s assumption ([8:6](Job.8.6)), Job’s prayer was **pure** because he was innocent ([Gen 20:5](Gen.20.5); [Isa 59:3](Isa.59.3)).
Job expected his suffering to prove fatal ([7:7](Job.7.7), [21](Job.7.21); [10:20-22](Job.10.20-Job.10.22)); he pleaded with God to reveal his innocence even if he died first.
Job’s **blood** would **cry out** that he had been innocent and that he had suffered undeservedly (cp. [Gen 4:10-11](Gen.4.10-Gen.4.11); [Isa 26:21](Isa.26.21); [Ezek 24:7-8](Ezek.24.7-Ezek.24.8)).

**my witness is in heaven:** Job wished for a benevolent third party who would **mediate** between him and God (see [9:32-35](Job.9.32-Job.9.35)). Job wanted an **advocate** from heaven ([16:19](Job.16.19); cp. [Zech 3:1](Zech.3.1)) who would eventually stand on the earth ([Job 19:25](Job.19.25); cp. [1 Sam 24:15](1Sam.24.15); [John 14:16](John.14.16), [26](John.14.26); [15:26](John.15.26); [16:7](John.16.7); [1 Jn 2:1](1John.2.1)).
**My spirit is crushed:** This can refer to a properly contrite attitude ([Ps 51:17](Ps.51.17)), but more often it connotes an unbearably sad heart ([Prov 18:14](Prov.18.14)).

**surrounded by mockers:** Laments typically describe mockery as the response of the wicked to the distress of the righteous ([Pss 22:7](Ps.22.7); [69:10-12](Ps.69.10-Ps.69.12); [89:50-52](Ps.89.50-Ps.89.52)). In wisdom literature, mockery is directed against the right behavior ([Prov 1:22](Prov.1.22); [9:7](Prov.9.7)).

**defend my innocence, O God** (literally *please keep my pledge with yourself*): A pledge (Hebrew *‘erabon*) can be a deposit guaranteeing payment ([Gen 38:17-20](Gen.38.17-Gen.38.20); [Exod 22:26-27](Exod.22.26-Exod.22.27); [Deut 24:10-14](Deut.24.10-Deut.24.14); see [Prov 20:16](Prov.20.16); [27:13](Prov.27.13)), so this might suggest atonement. It might also be another reference to Job’s desire for an advocate to plead his case (see study note on Job 16:19-21).
To **spit in** someone’s **face** was even more insulting than a slap ([16:10](Job.16.10)) because spit made the person unclean ([Num 12:14](Num.12.14)).
Some scholars view these verses as being out of place, but perhaps Job was ironically quoting his opponents’ words.
Job gave up on his comforters ([6:15-21](Job.6.15-Job.6.21); [13:4-5](Job.13.4-Job.13.5); [16:2-3](Job.16.2-Job.16.3); cp. [12:2](Job.12.2)) and believed he would die a hopeless death.
**to the grave** (Hebrew *to Sheol*): The realm of the dead was visualized as a house ([30:23](Job.30.23); [Ps 49:11](Ps.49.11); [Eccl 12:5](Eccl.12.5)).
**my father . . . mother . . . sister:** This bitter parody of a family reunion in a graveyard shows how Job envisioned his impending death.
**the grave** (literally *the bars of Sheol*): Sheol—the abode of the dead—was seen as having a barred gate, allowing no escape.
**How long before you stop talking?** Bildad addressed Job in the plural, perhaps meaning “people like you.”

**The light of the wicked will be snuffed out** could be a metaphor for a life of confused darkness ([Prov 4:19](Prov.4.19)); more likely, it indicates an early death ([Prov 13:9](Prov.13.9); [24:20](Prov.24.20)).
The **stride** that is **shortened** is the opposite of walking and running in the blessed life ([Prov 4:12](Prov.4.12)).
A series of hunting devices illustrates the biblical principle of retribution (see study note on 34:11).
Bildad applies the biblical principle of retribution ([18:8-10](Job.18.8-Job.18.10)) to Job, as do Eliphaz ([15:21-23](Job.15.21-Job.15.23)) and Zophar ([20:25](Job.20.25)).
**death devours:** Isaiah later reversed the figure and saw the Lord as swallowing up death ([Isa 25:8](Isa.25.8); see [1 Cor 15:54](1Cor.15.54)).
The image of **burning sulfur** recalls the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah ([Gen 19:24](Gen.19.24)) and suggests the fate of all the wicked ([Ps 11:6](Ps.11.6); [Rev 19:20](Rev.19.20); [21:8](Rev.21.8)).
Being forgotten by those who come later is a familiar curse against the wicked (see [18:19](Job.18.19); [Pss 34:16](Ps.34.16); [109:13](Ps.109.13); [Prov 10:7](Prov.10.7)).

This curse of childlessness (see [18:16](Job.18.16); [Pss 109:13](Ps.109.13); [Isa 14:21-22](Isa.14.21-Isa.14.22)) and Bildad’s earlier cruelty ([Job 8:4](Job.8.4)) show that he regarded Job’s condition as the just reward for his wickedness ([1:18-19](Job.1.18-Job.1.19)).
**in the west . . . in the east:** These phrases might refer to people from times past and times to come or to people from various places.
Bildad kept implying that Job had **rejected God** ([15:4](Job.15.4), [13](Job.15.13), [25](Job.15.25)).
The number **ten** did not represent a specific count but an indefinite large number (e.g., [Gen 31:7](Gen.31.7); [Lev 26:26](Lev.26.26); [Num 14:22](Num.14.22); [Dan 1:20](Dan.1.20)).

Job was convinced that justice had been delayed ([19:7](Job.19.7)) and that **God** had **wronged** him ([19:8-12](Job.19.8-Job.19.12)). Later, Elihu ([34:12](Job.34.12)) and God himself ([40:2](Job.40.2)) disagreed.
**capturing me in his net:** Job might have been responding to Bildad’s accusation ([18:8-10](Job.18.8-Job.18.10)).
**Help!** (literally *Violence!*): Cp. [Jer 20:8](Jer.20.8); [Hab 1:2-3](Hab.1.2-Hab.1.3).
**no one answers:** See [Ps 22:2](Ps.22.2); [Lam 3:8](Lam.3.8); [Hab 1:2-3](Hab.1.2-Hab.1.3).
**my own family:** Job might have been referring to his tribal line, his parents, his own children, or his siblings.
**escaped death by the skin of my teeth:** This is an idiom for a narrow escape; the Hebrew could also mean that Job was reduced to a skeleton with a toothy skull.
The **hand of God** had **struck** Job through the permission he gave to Satan ([1:11](Job.1.11); [2:5](Job.2.5)).
**persecute** (literally *pursue*): Job complained that God had tracked him like a hunter ([10:16](Job.10.16)) or a warrior ([16:13](Job.16.13)).

Job wanted his **words . . . inscribed on a monument***,* not in a book; Job desired a permanent record of his claim to innocence in response to Bildad’s assertion that he would be forgotten ([18:17](Job.18.17)).

Job’s faith in a **Redeemer** could find fulfillment only in Christ; the same was true of his request for an advocate ([9:33](Job.9.33)) and a witness in heaven ([16:19](Job.16.19)). The term “Redeemer” (Hebrew *go’el*) comes from both criminal and civil law. An individual could redeem or avenge wrongful bloodshed ([Num 35:12-18](Num.35.12-Num.35.18)) or redeem lost property, perhaps by buying back a slave or marrying the heir’s widow ([Lev 25:25](Lev.25.25), [47-49](Lev.25.47-Lev.25.49); [27:11-13](Lev.27.11-Lev.27.13); [Ruth 3:13](Ruth.3.13)). The Old Testament knew the Lord as redeemer ([Exod 6:6](Exod.6.6); [Pss 19:14](Ps.19.14); [103:4](Ps.103.4); [Prov 23:10-11](Prov.23.10-Prov.23.11); [Isa 43:1](Isa.43.1) \[“ransomed”\]; [Isa 54:5](Isa.54.5)); New Testament believers know the Redeemer as the Lord Jesus Christ ([Eph 1:7](Eph.1.7), [14](Eph.1.14); [Heb 9:12](Heb.9.12); [1 Pet 1:18](1Pet.1.18)). Job wanted his Redeemer to declare his innocence (see [Job 1:1](Job.1.1) and corresponding study note).
Job had faith that he would be vindicated even if death came first.

**I will see him for myself:** The thought is the same as the psalmist’s in “when I awake” ([Ps 17:15](Ps.17.15)). For Job, this hope could only be fulfilled in seeing God at the end of time ([Matt 5:8](Matt.5.8); [1 Cor 13:12](1Cor.13.12); [1 Jn 3:2](1John.3.2); [Rev 1:7](Rev.1.7)) in transformed flesh ([1 Cor 15:43-53](1Cor.15.43-1Cor.15.53); [Phil 3:21](Phil.3.21)).

Given the biblical principles against bearing false witness ([13:7-11](Job.13.7-Job.13.11); see [Matt 7:1-2](Matt.7.1-Matt.7.2); [Jas 4:11-12](Jas.4.11-Jas.4.12)), Job warned his friends that they should fear God’s judgment. They did eventually face his judgment, but they also received mercy ([Job 42:7-8](Job.42.7-Job.42.8)).
Because **stolen riches** are ill-gotten, they provide no lasting benefit ([20:18-21](Job.20.18-Job.20.21)).

**poisonous venom . . . cobras . . . viper:** In the end, the wicked are no longer deadly to others ([Matt 3:7](Matt.3.7); [Rom 3:13](Rom.3.13)) but only to themselves ([Prov 23:29-35](Prov.23.29-Prov.23.35)).
The **streams of olive oil** and **rivers of milk and honey** signify superabundant blessing ([Exod 5:19](Exod.5.19); [Deut 27:3](Deut.27.3); [Joel 3:18](Joel.3.18)).

Like the grave or death ([Prov 27:20](Prov.27.20); [30:15-16](Prov.30.15-Prov.30.16)), the wicked are **always greedy and never satisfied** ([Eccl 5:19](Eccl.5.19); [Isa 57:20-21](Isa.57.20-Isa.57.21); [Hab 2:5](Hab.2.5)).

The wicked cannot escape trouble (cp. [Isa 24:17-18](Isa.24.17-Isa.24.18); [Jer 15:2-3](Jer.15.2-Jer.15.3); [Amos 5:19](Amos.5.19); [9:1-2](Amos.9.1-Amos.9.2)). When they try to escape one threat, they fall victim to another.

**terrors of death:** Although the words “of death” are not in the Hebrew, they are implied because **the arrowhead glistens with blood** (literally *with gall*), indicating a deadly hit on a vital organ ([6:4](Job.6.4); [16:13](Job.16.13); [Ps 7:12](Ps.7.12)).

Images such as **deepest darkness** and **wildfire** are often associated with God’s presence ([Deut 4:11](Deut.4.11); [5:22-23](Deut.5.22-Deut.5.23); [Heb 12:18](Heb.12.18)) and especially with his judgment ([Exod 9:23-24](Exod.9.23-Exod.9.24); [10:21-29](Exod.10.21-Exod.10.29)).

Job’s friends insisted that they were delivering God’s own message of comfort ([15:11](Job.15.11)), but Job found no comfort in their words ([16:2](Job.16.2)), so he asked for the **consolation** of their attentive silence (see [13:5](Job.13.5)).

**When I think about what I am saying:** Job was dismayed by his horrible task of complaining against God ([13:3](Job.13.3), [15-16](Job.13.15-Job.13.16), [22](Job.13.22); [23:1-5](Job.23.1-Job.23.5)) and discussing his terrors ([6:4](Job.6.4); [27:20](Job.27.20); [30:15](Job.30.15)).

**My body trembles:** This reaction resembles that of Habakkuk ([Hab 1:5](Hab.1.5); [3:16](Hab.3.16)), Ezekiel ([Ezek 3:14](Ezek.3.14)), and Daniel ([Dan 8:27](Dan.8.27); [10:8-9](Dan.10.8-Dan.10.9)).

In spite of assertions by Eliphaz ([5:4](Job.5.4)), Bildad ([18:19](Job.18.19)), and Zophar ([20:10](Job.20.10)), Job noted that the wicked enjoy **children** and **grandchildren***,* which should be the reward of the righteous ([Prov 17:6](Prov.17.6)) but was apparently not going to be his own reward ([Job 1:18-19](Job.1.18-Job.1.19); but see [42:13-16](Job.42.13-Job.42.16)).

**light of the wicked never seems to be extinguished:** Job countered Bildad ([18:5-6](Job.18.5-Job.18.6), [18](Job.18.18)) and standard wisdom ([Prov 13:9](Prov.13.9); [20:20](Prov.20.20); [24:20](Job.24.20); see God’s remarks, [Job 38:15](Job.38.15)).
**you say:** Job was quoting and rebutting his friends’ arguments.

**God will punish their children:** These were the words of Eliphaz ([5:4](Job.5.4)) and Zophar ([20:10](Job.20.10)), but Job thought God **should punish the ones who sin** (see [Ezek 18:19-20](Ezek.18.19-Ezek.18.20)).
The rhetorical answer is that no one **can teach a lesson to God** ([Isa 40:13-14](Isa.40.13-Isa.40.14); [45:9](Isa.45.9); [Rom 11:34](Rom.11.34); [1 Cor 2:16](1Cor.2.16)).

The **most powerful** might refer to angels or demons ([1 Cor 6:3](1Cor.6.3); [2 Pet 2:4](2Pet.2.4); [Jude 1:6](Jude.1.6); [Rev 20:1-3](Rev.20.1-Rev.20.3)) or, more likely, to the powerful on earth ([Job 34:17-19](Job.34.17-Job.34.19)).
**vigorous and fit** (literally *the marrow of his bones \[is\] moist*): Bones were thought to be the seat of health.
**in bitter poverty:** Job repeatedly complained about the apparent futility of existence ([3:20](Job.3.20); [7:11](Job.7.11); [9:18](Job.9.18); [10:1](Job.10.1)).
**eaten by the same maggots:** Cp. [17:14](Job.17.14); [Isa 14:11](Isa.14.11); see [Job 19:26](Job.19.26).
**houses have vanished because of their sins:** Job was echoing Bildad ([8:22](Job.8.22)), Eliphaz ([15:34](Job.15.34)), and Zophar ([20:26](Job.20.26)).
**the earth gives sweet repose:** Job viewed death as a relief ([3:17-18](Job.3.17-Job.3.18)).
They told **lies** about Job ([13:4](Job.13.4)) and about God ([42:7](Job.42.7)).
In this third round of speeches, Job’s friends explicitly accuse Job of being among the wicked and sharing their fate.

Eliphaz did not understand that God would **gain** pleasure from Job’s righteousness ([1:8](Job.1.8); [2:3](Job.2.3)), as he does from every righteous person ([1 Chr 29:17](1Chr.29.17); [Ps 147:10-11](Ps.147.10-Ps.147.11); [Prov 11:1](Prov.11.1), [20](Prov.11.20); [12:22](Prov.12.22)). God would also gain glory from Job’s steadfast faith, which emphasized the lie behind Satan’s challenge ([Job 1:9-12](Job.1.9-Job.1.12); [2:4-6](Job.2.4-Job.2.6)).
Job steadfastly claimed that he was **perfect** ([23:10-12](Job.23.10-Job.23.12)), as did God himself ([1:1](Job.1.1), [8](Job.1.8); [2:3](Job.2.3)).

Demanding **clothing as security** for **lent money** was forbidden by the law and condemned by the prophets ([Exod 22:26-27](Exod.22.26-Exod.22.27); [Deut 24:10-13](Deut.24.10-Deut.24.13); [Ezek 18:7-8](Ezek.18.7-Ezek.18.8); [Amos 2:8](Amos.2.8)). In contrast, Job had provided clothing for the poor ([Job 31:19-20](Job.31.19-Job.31.20)).

The Old Testament gives Israel the responsibility of caring for **widows** and **orphans** ([Deut 10:18](Deut.10.18); [14:29](Deut.14.29)) and repeatedly condemns their neglect as the worst of social evils ([Exod 22:22-24](Exod.22.22-Exod.22.24); [Deut 27:19](Deut.27.19)). Job agreed that it was wicked ([Job 24:3](Job.24.3), [21](Job.24.21)) but claimed that he was innocent ([29:12-13](Job.29.12-Job.29.13); [31:16-18](Job.31.16-Job.31.18), [21](Job.31.21)).
**That’s why:** Job had not claimed that **God can’t see***,* but others have ([Pss 10:11](Ps.10.11); [73:11](Ps.73.11); [94:7](Ps.94.7)).
**I will have nothing to do with that kind of thinking:** Eliphaz threw Job’s words back at him ([21:16b](Job.21.16)).

**The righteous will be happy to see the wicked destroyed:** They will be glad to see justice done and injustices avenged (see also [Ps 58:10-11](Ps.58.10-Ps.58.11); [Rev 19:1-4](Rev.19.1-Rev.19.4)). Eliphaz’s sentiment neglected God’s desire that sinful people repent (see [Ezek 33:11](Ezek.33.11)).
The term **instructions** (Hebrew *torah,* “law,” [Deut 17:11](Deut.17.11)), used in Job only here, frequently refers to the Pentateuch (Genesis—Deuteronomy).
**Listen . . . store:** See [Deut 4:1-2](Deut.4.1-Deut.4.2); [6:6-9](Deut.6.6-Deut.6.9); [Ps 119:11](Ps.119.11); [Prov 2:1-9](Prov.2.1-Prov.2.9). Job had done this ([Job 23:12](Job.23.12)).

**return to the Almighty:** Bildad ([8:5-6](Job.8.5-Job.8.6)) and Zophar ([11:13-14](Job.11.13-Job.11.14)) had already misapplied this biblical principle ([Isa 55:6-7](Isa.55.6-Isa.55.7); [Hos 14:1-2](Hos.14.1-Hos.14.2); [Zech 1:3](Zech.1.3); [Acts 26:20](Acts.26.20)), and now Eliphaz also misapplies it.

**precious gold** (literally *Ophir*): Ophir was probably located in southern Arabia (see [1 Kgs 9:28](1Kgs.9.28); [22:48](1Kgs.22.48)). The gold of Ophir was the standard in fine gold ([Isa 13:12](Isa.13.12)); queens wore it at weddings ([Ps 45:9](Ps.45.9)).

God promises to be his people’s **treasure** ([Ps 16:5](Ps.16.5); [Isa 33:6](Isa.33.6); [Matt 19:21](Matt.19.21); [Mark 10:21](Mark.10.21)); although they possess nothing, they will be rich ([2 Cor 6:10](2Cor.6.10); [Jas 2:5](Jas.2.5)).
Ironically, Job **will pray***,* God **will hear***,* and Eliphaz will reap the benefits ([42:8](Job.42.8)).

**you will fulfill your vows:** Vows were often stimulated by repentance and forgiveness ([Hos 14:2](Hos.14.2); [Jon 1:16](Jonah.1.16); [2:9](Jonah.2.9)) and when seeking divine intervention ([Judg 11:29-40](Judg.11.29-Judg.11.40); [1 Sam 1:1-28](1Sam.1.1-1Sam.1.28)). Vows are binding ([Num 30:2](Num.30.2); [Deut 23:23](Deut.23.23); [Pss 22:25](Ps.22.25); [61:5](Ps.61.5), [8](Ps.61.8); [116:14](Ps.116.14), [18](Ps.116.18); [Eccl 5:4-5](Eccl.5.4-Eccl.5.5)).

This difficult text probably conveys the effectiveness of a righteous man’s prayer. The principle ([Pss 34:15](Ps.34.15), [17](Ps.34.17); [145:18](Ps.145.18); [Prov 15:8](Prov.15.8), [29](Job.15.29); [Jas 5:16](Jas.5.16)) is illustrated throughout Scripture (see, e.g., [Gen 18:23-32](Gen.18.23-Gen.18.32); [19:29](Gen.19.29); [20:7](Gen.20.7), [17](Gen.20.17); [32:28](Gen.32.28); [Exod 9:28-32](Exod.9.28-Exod.9.32); [17:11](Exod.17.11); [32:10-14](Exod.32.10-Exod.32.14); [Rom 5:19](Rom.5.19)).
Job dropped the doubt he had expressed earlier ([9:14-20](Job.9.14-Job.9.20), [32](Job.9.32)) and here expressed confidence that he could successfully present his **complaint**.

**present my arguments:** Job wanted to make his **case** with God ([13:3](Job.13.3), [18](Job.13.18), [22](Job.13.22); [16:21](Job.16.21); [31:35](Job.31.35)); Abraham pled directly with God regarding Sodom ([Gen 18:25-32](Gen.18.25-Gen.18.32)), and Moses did the same for Israel ([Exod 32:12-13](Exod.32.12-Exod.32.13); [Num 14:13-19](Num.14.13-Num.14.19)).

Earlier, Job had believed that God was too strong for him to summon ([9:19](Job.9.19)), so he had requested an arbiter ([9:33-34](Job.9.33-Job.9.34)) and asked God not to terrify him ([13:21](Job.13.21)). Here he expressed more hope that God would grant him **a fair hearing**.
**acquitted:** Job did not want to be pardoned as a guilty man but to be declared innocent ([13:18](Job.13.18); see [Pss 17:2-3](Ps.17.2-Ps.17.3); [26:1-3](Ps.26.1-Ps.26.3)).

**tests me:** Job did not want the kind of chastising that would cleanse him like a refiner’s fire ([Prov 17:3](Prov.17.3); [Zech 13:9](Zech.13.9); [Mal 3:2-3](Mal.3.2-Mal.3.3)). He wanted an examination that would prove that he had been as **pure as gold** and did not need to amend his life ([Job 22:23](Job.22.23)).

Job had complained earlier of being plunged into **darkness** ([Job 19:8](Job.19.8)); Eliphaz ([15:22](Job.15.22); [22:1](Job.22.1)) and Bildad ([18:6](Job.18.6), [18](Job.18.18)) ascribed this fate to the wicked.

**bring . . . to judgment** (literally *set times*): The times for God’s judgment are set ([Eccl 3:17](Eccl.3.17); [8:6](Eccl.8.6); [Dan 2:21](Dan.2.21); [Luke 21:22-24](Luke.21.22-Luke.21.24)), but they are not known to us ([Acts 1:7](Acts.1.7)). They will be revealed at the proper moment ([1 Thes 5:1-28](1Thess.5.1-1Thess.5.28); [1 Tim 6:15](1Tim.6.15)).
This inventory of criminal behaviors focuses first on crimes against the weak ([24:2-12](Job.24.2-Job.24.12)) and then on the criminals themselves ([24:13-17](Job.24.13-Job.24.17)).

The law, wisdom literature, and prophecy all condemned the **moving** of **boundary markers** ([Deut 19:14](Deut.19.14); [27:17](Deut.27.17); [Prov 22:28](Prov.22.28); [23:10](Prov.23.10); see study note on Hos 5:10).

The law did not allow seizing necessary belongings as **security** or collateral **for a loan** ([22:6-9](Job.22.6-Job.22.9); [Deut 24:6](Deut.24.6), [10-13](Deut.24.10-Deut.24.13), [17-21](Deut.24.17-Deut.24.21)).

**glean in the vineyards of the wicked:** Job was depicting the desperate condition of the poor. If their fields had been stolen like Naboth’s vineyard ([24:2](Job.24.2); see [1 Kgs 21:1-29](1Kgs.21.1-1Kgs.21.29)), the poor would harvest for the thieving owners what should have been their own crops; instead of owning the whole crop, they would get just the leftover pickings for themselves. Perhaps the point is that the poor were forced to glean from the fields of wicked people who left no gleanings ([Lev 19:10](Lev.19.10); [23:22](Lev.23.22)), instead of being able to glean from the righteous, who leave something for the poor ([Lev 19:9-10](Lev.19.9-Lev.19.10); [23:22](Lev.23.22); [Ruth 2:1-23](Ruth.2.1-Ruth.2.23)).

Unjust lenders sometimes left debtors **without clothing or covering**, which they had seized as collateral on loans ([22:6](Job.22.6); [Exod 22:26-27](Exod.22.26-Exod.22.27); [Deut 24:11-13](Deut.24.11-Deut.24.13); [Amos 2:8](Amos.2.8)).
**widow’s child . . . security for a loan:** See [2 Kgs 4:1](2Kgs.4.1); [Neh 5:1-5](Neh.5.1-Neh.5.5); [Matt 18:25](Matt.18.25).
**without being allowed to taste it:** These words, which are not in the original text, are implied by the parallel with *starving* and **suffer from thirst**.

To force workers to **tread in the winepress as they suffer from thirst** violates the principle of letting workers enjoy some of the produce they are harvesting (see [Deut 25:4](Deut.25.4); cp. [2 Tim 2:6](2Tim.2.6)).
