**ignores their moaning:** It appeared to Job that contrary to God’s own character ([Exod 2:23-24](Exod.2.23-Exod.2.24); [Ps 12:5](Ps.12.5)), God neither relieved the plight of the wronged ([Job 24:2-12](Job.24.2-Job.24.12)) nor hindered the wicked from harming their victims ([24:13-17](Job.24.13-Job.24.17)).

These sentiments appear to oppose Job’s observations, so some scholars suggest that they were the words of Bildad or Zophar. However, Job might have been pronouncing curses on the wicked, sarcastically quoting his friends’ views, or saying that the fate of the wicked presented by Eliphaz ([5:2-7](Job.5.2-Job.5.7); [15:17-25](Job.15.17-Job.15.25)), Bildad ([8:8-19](Job.8.8-Job.8.19); [18:5-21](Job.18.5-Job.18.21)), and Zophar ([20:4-29](Job.20.4-Job.20.29)) also overtakes the righteous ([21:23-26](Job.21.23-Job.21.26)).

Eliphaz had said that it is nearly impossible to **be innocent** or **pure** ([4:17-19](Job.4.17-Job.4.19); [15:14-16](Job.15.14-Job.15.16)), and then only after suffering ([22:21-23](Job.22.21-Job.22.23)). Bildad claimed that only the totally blameless could hope to be pure ([8:20](Job.8.20)).

Job’s friends had not **helped** him ([12:2](Job.12.2); [16:4](Job.16.4)). Bildad’s denial that acquittal was possible hit Job’s most sensitive nerve ([10:1-7](Job.10.1-Job.10.7); [13:3](Job.13.3), [13-19](Job.13.13-Job.13.19); [16:18-21](Job.16.18-Job.16.21); [19:23-27](Job.19.23-Job.19.27); [23:2-7](Job.23.2-Job.23.7)).

Eliphaz ([4:15](Job.4.15)), Zophar ([20:3](Job.20.3)), and Elihu ([32:18](Job.32.18); [33:4](Job.33.4)) all claimed to be prompted by the proper **spirit** (see [Jer 29:8-9](Jer.29.8-Jer.29.9); [1 Cor 12:10](1Cor.12.10); [1 Jn 4:1](1John.4.1)).
**The underworld** (Hebrew *Sheol*), the abode of all the dead, is located **beneath the waters** of the sea.
**The place of destruction** (Hebrew *Abaddon*) existed specifically for the wicked.

The Hebrew *tsapon* (“north,” [Gen 13:14](Gen.13.14)) sometimes refers to the **northern** mountain of the Canaanite gods (the Canaanite equivalent of Olympus); here the NLT understands it to refer to the **sky***,* stretched out **over empty space** (see [Gen 1:6-8](Gen.1.6-Gen.1.8); [Ps 104:2-3](Ps.104.2-Ps.104.3); [Isa 40:22-23](Isa.40.22-Isa.40.23)).

Mountains at the edge of the horizon might be the **foundations** (or “pillars,” [Judg 16:25-26](Judg.16.25-Judg.16.26)) **of heaven** or the earth ([Job 9:6](Job.9.6)). They were thought to reach from below the waters of the sea ([Jon 2:6](Jonah.2.6)) and up to the clouds to support the vaults of heaven.

**the sea grew calm** (cp. [Exod 14:21](Exod.14.21); [Mark 4:39](Mark.4.39)): Or *the sea was stirred up* (cp. [Isa 51:15](Isa.51.15); [Jer 31:35](Jer.31.35)). In either interpretation, God performed a miracle on behalf of his people.

**crushed the great sea monster:** God’s dominance over the sea demythologized popular beliefs about the sea’s divinity. See also [Pss 74:13-14](Ps.74.13-Ps.74.14); [89:9-10](Ps.89.9-Ps.89.10); [Isa 27:1](Isa.27.1); [51:9-10](Isa.51.9-Isa.51.10).
**His Spirit** (or *wind*): God’s authority clears the skies after a storm ([26:12](Job.26.12)).

The **gliding serpent** corresponds to Yam and Rahab (see study note on 7:12); it provides background for the image of Satan as a dragon ([Isa 27:1](Isa.27.1); also [Ps 74:13-14](Ps.74.13-Ps.74.14); see [Gen 3:15](Gen.3.15); [Rom 16:20](Rom.16.20); [Rev 12:9](Rev.12.9); [20:2](Rev.20.2)).
**Job continued speaking**, no longer responding to the three friends but returning to the themes of his opening statement ([3:1-26](Job.3.1-Job.3.26)).

The Bible permits a **vow by the living God** ([Ruth 3:13](Ruth.3.13); [1 Sam 20:21](1Sam.20.21); [25:26](1Sam.25.26); [1 Kgs 17:1](1Kgs.17.1); [18:15](1Kgs.18.15); [Jer 4:2](Jer.4.2)), although sometimes it is done foolishly or falsely ([1 Sam 14:39](1Sam.14.39), [45](1Sam.14.45); [Jer 5:2](Jer.5.2)).
Elihu later criticized Job for saying that God had **taken away** his **rights** ([Job 34:5](Job.34.5)).

**embittered . . . soul** ([7:11](Job.7.11); [10:1](Job.10.1); [21:25](Job.21.25)): Cp. Naomi ([Ruth 1:20-21](Ruth.1.20-Ruth.1.21)) and the widow from Shunem after the loss of her son ([2 Kgs 4:27](2Kgs.4.27)).

Job considered it profane and reprehensible to **concede that** his friends were right. Condemning the innocent, as they were doing to him, was an abomination ([Exod 23:7](Exod.23.7); [Prov 6:16-19](Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19); [17:15](Prov.17.15)).
Some interpreters see a new speech here and ascribe it to Zophar because otherwise Zophar has no speech in this cycle.

This section is a self-contained speech. No speaker is listed, so it could be a continuation of the preceding words. However, some consider this a poetic interlude by the author of Job that sums up the argument to this point, emphasizes the failure of human wisdom, and lays the foundation for the Lord’s speeches.
Miners **melted** rock by burning a **fire** in a mine for days or even weeks to melt out the ore. Some alternated fire with cold water to split the rocks.
Wisdom does not originate **among the living**. God is the source of true wisdom ([28:23-28](Job.28.23-Job.28.28)).
The metals, gemstones, and glass listed here were precious in the ancient world, but the speaker says that wisdom is much more precious than wealth.

When God **looks throughout the whole earth** ([28:23](Job.28.23)), he sees his own wisdom expressed in his creation. God later showcased his wisdom for Job when he took him on a cosmic tour (chs [38–41](Job.38.1-Job.41.34)).
**fear of the Lord** (Hebrew, *’adonay*): In Job, this name for God appears only here, which might be one argument for understanding ch [28](Job.28.1-Job.28.28) as the narrator’s own poem.

Job contrasts his former happiness, honor, and wealth (ch [29](Job.29.1-Job.29.25)) with his loss of social dignity and divine friendship (ch [30](Job.30.1-Job.30.31)). He concludes his speech with wide-ranging oaths of innocence (ch [31](Job.31.1-Job.31.40)).

Although elsewhere Job uses the Hebrew *shamar* to describe what he perceived as God’s oppressive surveillance ([10:14](Job.10.14); [13:27](Job.13.27); [14:16](Job.14.16)), here it refers to God’s kindly **care** (“watch(es) over,” [Ps 121:3-8](Ps.121.3-Ps.121.8)).
The **city gate** was a town’s administrative center (see [Ruth 4:1-2](Ruth.4.1-Ruth.4.2), [11](Ruth.4.11)).

Job described his **righteousness** in royal terms. A **robe** is a common biblical image for righteousness ([Ps 132:9](Ps.132.9); [Isa 59:17](Isa.59.17); [61:10](Isa.61.10); [Rom 13:14](Rom.13.14); [Rev 19:8](Rev.19.8)).
Job actively searched out and **assisted strangers who needed help**.

**after a long, good life** (literally *after I have counted my days like sand*): Job thought the length of his years would signify God’s blessing, like the great number of Abraham’s offspring ([Gen 15:5](Gen.15.5); [32:12](Gen.32.12)) or the abundance of Joseph’s supplies in Egypt ([Gen 41:49](Gen.41.49)).

In the past, Job had **comforted those who mourned** ([4:3-4](Job.4.3-Job.4.4)). This verse is a prophetic mandate closely associated with the work of the Messiah ([Isa 40:1](Isa.40.1); [61:1-3](Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3); [Luke 4:18-19](Luke.4.18-Luke.4.19); cp. [2 Cor 1:3-4](2Cor.1.3-2Cor.1.4)).

In the past, the most honorable members of society spoke well of Job ([29:11](Job.29.11)); now, the least honorable mocked him ([30:1](Job.30.1)) and spit in his face ([30:10](Job.30.10)). Cp. [Pss 35:15](Ps.35.15); [69:12](Ps.69.12); [Mark 14:65](Mark.14.65); [15:17-20](Mark.15.17-Mark.15.20).

**live in frightening ravines, in caves and among the rocks:** The wretched life of Job’s mockers resembled Israel’s situation under Midianite oppression ([Judg 6:2](Judg.6.2)), David’s life as he fled from Saul ([1 Sam 22:1-2](1Sam.22.1-1Sam.22.2)), and Elijah’s life as he awaited the Lord’s instruction ([1 Kgs 17:3-8](1Kgs.17.3-1Kgs.17.8)).
To **spit in** someone’s **face** was to display revulsion or contempt ([Deut 25:9](Deut.25.9); [Isa 50:6](Isa.50.6); [Matt 26:67](Matt.26.67); [27:30](Matt.27.30); [Mark 14:65](Mark.14.65)).
The series of images presented here is drawn from a military advance against a fortified city. Job had already used this image for God’s attack on him ([19:10-12](Job.19.10-Job.19.12)).
The word translated **traps** might refer to siege ramps raised against a city’s walls.

**God grabs . . . the collar of my coat:** The Hebrew in this verse is difficult to translate; it could mean that Job feels like he is in a chokehold and is about to be thrown into the mud (cp. [30:19](Job.30.19)).
**dust and ashes:** Earlier, Job was sitting “among the ashes” in anguish ([2:8](Job.2.8)); later, he would “sit in dust and ashes to show . . . repentance” ([42:6](Job.42.6)).
**you don’t answer:** This was Job’s frequent complaint ([9:16](Job.9.16); [19:7](Job.19.7); [23:2-9](Job.23.2-Job.23.9); [31:35](Job.31.35)), which God soon answered ([38:1](Job.38.1)).
Job felt tossed **into the whirlwind** and blown about like worthless straw or chaff ([9:17](Job.9.17); [21:18](Job.21.18); [27:21](Job.27.21); [Ps 1:4](Ps.1.4); [Isa 17:13](Isa.17.13)).

Before his testing began, Job had been respected in **the public square** ([29:7-10](Job.29.7-Job.29.10), [21-25](Job.29.21-Job.29.25)); he helped others who were in need ([29:11-17](Job.29.11-Job.29.17)).
**I am considered:** Job might have been expressing what he thought of himself, how others viewed him, or both.

By claiming that he was **a brother to jackals and a companion to owls***,* Job might have been describing himself as in the throes of lament ([Mic 1:8](Mic.1.8)). Jackals were associated with desolation or ruin (see [Ps 63:10](Ps.63.10); [Isa 13:22](Isa.13.22); [34:13](Isa.34.13); [35:7](Isa.35.7); [Jer 9:11](Jer.9.11); [10:22](Jer.10.22); [49:33](Jer.49.33); [51:37](Jer.51.37); [Lam 5:18](Lam.5.18); [Ezek 13:4](Ezek.13.4); [Mal 1:3](Mal.1.3)).
The **skin** of a person who lived in comfortable circumstances was protected from the sun and wind; **dark** skin indicated physical and social decline ([Lam 4:8](Lam.4.8); [5:10](Lam.5.10)).

Job called down curses on himself if he were guilty of the accusations made against him. Except for his mention of idolatry ([31:26-27](Job.31.26-Job.31.27)), Job addressed his fidelity to God in terms of the second half of the Ten Commandments, summarized by the command to “love your neighbor as yourself” ([Lev 19:18](Lev.19.18); [Rom 13:9](Rom.13.9)).

Job’s **covenant with** his **eyes** included a self-cursing oath (cp. [Matt 5:28-29](Matt.5.28-Matt.5.29)). Perhaps lust of the eyes was at the head of Job’s list because the eye is the first instrument of sin ([Gen 3:6](Gen.3.6)).

To **look with lust at a young woman** violates the spirit of the seventh ([Deut 5:18](Deut.5.18), see [Matt 5:27-28](Matt.5.27-Matt.5.28)), and potentially the tenth ([Deut 5:21](Deut.5.21)), commandment.

If Job had **lied to anyone** as part of a business deal, it would violate the eighth commandment ([Deut 5:19](Deut.5.19)); if it occurred in court, it would violate the ninth ([Deut 5:20](Deut.5.20)). This sin would merit fiery judgment ([Rev 21:8](Rev.21.8)).
If Job **lusted for what** his **eyes** had **seen***,* he would violate the tenth commandment ([Deut 5:21](Deut.5.21)).
**then let someone else eat:** This was a self-curse.

Whether she **seduced** him or he waited for her ([24:15-16](Job.24.15-Job.24.16)), if Job **lusted for** his **neighbor’s wife** he would break the seventh ([Deut 5:18](Deut.5.18), [Matt 5:27-28](Matt.5.27-Matt.5.28)) and tenth ([Deut 5:21](Deut.5.21)) commandments.
**serve:** Literally *grind for*. This might refer to servitude ([Exod 11:5](Exod.11.5)) or to sexual intercourse.

The Hebrew term *zimmah* (**shameful sin**) is associated with sexual crimes such as incest (“wicked act,” [Lev 18:17](Lev.18.17)), gang-rape (“terrible . . . crime,” [Judg 20:6](Judg.20.6)), and prostitution ([Ezek 23:49](Ezek.23.49)).
The association of **fire** with **hell** or the grave is rare in the Old Testament (cp. [Deut 32:22](Deut.32.22)).
**unfair to . . . servants:** This might refer to violations of the fourth commandment ([Deut 5:12-15](Deut.5.12-Deut.5.15)).
**God created both me and my servants:** Job extended the implications of being created in God’s image to the poor ([Prov 14:31](Prov.14.31); [22:2](Prov.22.2)) and even to slaves.
**knowing the judges would take my side:** Job was respected and regarded as a member of the elite class ([29:7-10](Job.29.7-Job.29.10)).

If an **arm** was used in sinful action ([31:21](Job.31.21)), having it **torn from its socket** would be a fitting punishment and **better than facing God’s judgment** (cp. [Matt 5:28-30](Matt.5.28-Matt.5.30)).

**Have I put my trust in . . . my gold:** Job left the consequence of this oath unstated because the if-then pattern was now established ([31:5-23](Job.31.5-Job.31.23)). He rejected Eliphaz’s implied judgment ([22:24-25](Job.22.24-Job.22.25); see [Pss 52:7](Ps.52.7); [62:10](Ps.62.10); [1 Tim 6:10](1Tim.6.10), [17](1Tim.6.17)).

Like adultery (cp. [31:1](Job.31.1), [9-12](Job.31.9-Job.31.12)), worshiping the sun and moon was a capital crime. Both were sins of the eye that enticed the heart, and both types of sin were tried before judges.

**Have I looked at the sun . . . or the moon:** This oath denies violation (cp. [Jer 8:2](Jer.8.2); [44:17](Jer.44.17); [Ezek 8:16](Ezek.8.16); [Acts 7:43](Acts.7.43)) of the first commandment ([Deut 5:7](Deut.5.7); see [Deut 4:19](Deut.4.19); [17:2-7](Deut.17.2-Deut.17.7)).
**secretly enticed in my heart:** See [31:9](Job.31.9).
**throw kisses at them in worship:** Cp. [1 Kgs 19:18](1Kgs.19.18); [Hos 13:2](Hos.13.2).
In Israel, **the judges** (see [31:11](Job.31.11)) were to punish idol worship by execution ([Deut 17:2-7](Deut.17.2-Deut.17.7)).
Denying **the God of heaven** violated the first commandment ([Deut 5:7](Deut.5.7)).
**rejoiced when disaster struck my enemies:** See [Prov 24:17-18](Prov.24.17-Prov.24.18); cp. [2 Sam 16:5-8](2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.8).
**Cursing anyone** violated the spirit of the sixth commandment ([Deut 5:17](Deut.5.17); see [Matt 5:21-22](Matt.5.21-Matt.5.22)).
It was against God’s will to ask **for revenge** ([Matt 5:43-44](Matt.5.43-Matt.5.44); [Rom 12:14](Rom.12.14); [Jas 3:6-10](Jas.3.6-Jas.3.10); [1 Pet 3:9](1Pet.3.9)).

**never turned away a stranger:** The Old Testament values hospitality ([Gen 18:1-13](Gen.18.1-Gen.18.13); [19:2-3](Gen.19.2-Gen.19.3); [Judg 19:20-21](Judg.19.20-Judg.19.21)), and the New Testament commands it ([Matt 25:35](Matt.25.35); [Rom 12:13](Rom.12.13); [1 Tim 3:2](1Tim.3.2); [Heb 13:2](Heb.13.2); [1 Pet 4:9](1Pet.4.9)).
**sign my name:** Job wanted to make the proceedings official ([19:23-24](Job.19.23-Job.19.24)).
**face the accusation proudly** (literally *carry it on my shoulder;* cp. [Exod 28:12](Exod.28.12); [Isa 22:22](Isa.22.22)): He would take full responsibility for his actions.
A **prince** who had been wrongly accused had the right to **come before** his king to make an appeal.
The **land** was the chief witness to crimes committed upon it ([20:27](Job.20.27); see [Gen 4:10](Gen.4.10); cp. [Jas 5:4](Jas.5.4)).
**let thistles grow:** Job’s curse on himself echoed God’s primal curse on Adam ([Gen 3:17-18](Gen.3.17-Gen.3.18); cp. [Isa 7:25](Isa.7.25); [Zeph 2:9](Zeph.2.9)).

Having completed three cycles of speeches between Job and his three friends, we now hear from a new voice. Elihu has not been previously introduced, but he is a young man who has listened to everything the others have said.
**the Buzite:** Buz had connections with Aram ([Gen 22:21](Gen.22.21)) and Arabia ([Jer 25:23](Jer.25.23)), as did *Uz* ([Job 1:1](Job.1.1)).
Elihu repeatedly stated that he was **angry***;* he probably regarded his anger as righteous zeal ([Ps 69:9](Ps.69.9)).
Elihu’s deference to elders followed a well-known principle (see also [12:12](Job.12.12); [15:10](Job.15.10); [Lev 19:32](Lev.19.32); [1 Tim 5:1](1Tim.5.1); [1 Pet 5:5](1Pet.5.5)).

The **spirit within people** might not be the prophetic Spirit that Elihu later appeals to ([33:14-15](Job.33.14-Job.33.15)), as Eliphaz had done ([4:12-17](Job.4.12-Job.4.17); cp. [32:18-20](Job.32.18-Job.32.20)). This spirit might simply exist by virtue of creation ([33:4](Job.33.4); [Gen 2:7](Gen.2.7); [Acts 17:25](Acts.17.25)).

As translated, the phrase **you sit there . . . you are silent** is addressed to Job’s friends. An alternate translation is *they sit there . . . they are silent,* in which case Elihu is speaking to Job about his friends.
The length of Elihu’s speech ([32:1–37:24](Job.32.1-Job.37.24)) demonstrates that he truly was **full of pent-up words**.

Elihu probably thought **the spirit** (Hebrew *ruakh*) **within** him was prophetic urgency ([32:8](Job.32.8), [19-20](Job.32.19-Job.32.20); [Ps 39:3](Ps.39.3)), but the reader might find him full of *wind* (Hebrew *ruakh;* see study note on Job 15:2-3).
Like Zophar, Elihu **must speak to find relief** (cp. [20:2](Job.20.2)).
**Listen:** Elihu begged to be heard ([33:1](Job.33.1); [34:2](Job.34.2), [16](Job.34.16)), which is what Job had also sought ([13:6](Job.13.6)).
By inviting Job to **make** his **case**, Elihu acted as though he were God, or at least the arbiter that Job had been seeking ([9:32-35](Job.9.32-Job.9.35)).

**you don’t need to be afraid of me** (literally *my terror shall not make you afraid*): God’s terrors ([6:4](Job.6.4); [7:14](Job.7.14); [9:34](Job.9.34); [13:21](Job.13.21); [23:15](Job.23.15)) had been thrown in Job’s face by Eliphaz ([15:21](Job.15.21), [24](Job.15.24); [22:10](Job.22.10)), Bildad ([18:11](Job.18.11), [14](Job.18.14)), and Zophar ([20:25](Job.20.25)).
Elihu promised not to **come down hard on** Job, but later he broke his word ([34:7-9](Job.34.7-Job.34.9), [33-37](Job.34.33-Job.34.37)).

Job frequently complained about God’s surveillance ([7:20](Job.7.20); [10:14](Job.10.14); [13:27](Job.13.27)); he wanted relief from having his **every move** scrutinized ([14:16](Job.14.16); [29:2](Job.29.2)).
Job’s central complaint was that God **does not respond** ([9:16](Job.9.16); [19:7](Job.19.7); [23:2-7](Job.23.2-Job.23.7)).
**from crossing over the river of death:** This phrase may also be translated *from passing* \[i.e., *dying*\] *by the sword.* Both translations fit the context (cp. [36:12](Job.36.12)).
**angels of death wait for them:** Cp. [Exod 12:23](Exod.12.23); [2 Sam 24:16](2Sam.24.16); [1 Cor 10:10](1Cor.10.10).
An **angel from heaven** would **intercede,** taking the role of the mediator Job longed for (see [5:1](Job.5.1); [9:33-34](Job.9.33-Job.9.34); [16:18-21](Job.16.18-Job.16.21)).
The **ransom** is ultimately **found** in Christ ([Matt 20:28](Matt.20.28); [Rom 3:24-25](Rom.3.24-Rom.3.25); [1 Tim 2:6](1Tim.2.6); [1 Pet 1:18-19](1Pet.1.18-1Pet.1.19)).
**God will receive him with joy:** Cp. [Num 6:24-26](Num.6.24-Num.6.26); [Ps 67:1](Ps.67.1); [Acts 2:28](Acts.2.28); [Jude 1:24](Jude.1.24).

For Elihu to say that he was **anxious to see** Job **justified** sounds ironic; he had entered the discussion in the first place “because Job refused to admit that he had sinned” ([32:1-5](Job.32.1-Job.32.5)).

**ear tests . . . mouth distinguishes:** Elihu echoed Job’s earlier complaint about the other counselors’ weak argument that “wisdom belongs to the aged” ([12:11-12](Job.12.11-Job.12.12); see [6:30](Job.6.30); [Heb 5:14](Heb.5.14)).
Job had claimed to be **innocent:** See [9:20-21](Job.9.20-Job.9.21); [13:18](Job.13.18); [27:6](Job.27.6).
Eliphaz had accused Job of being a **liar** ([15:5](Job.15.5)), fulfilling Job’s earlier worry ([6:28-29](Job.6.28-Job.6.29)).

**My suffering** (literally *My arrow*): For the link with the Lord’s arrows, see [6:4](Job.6.4); [16:13](Job.16.13); [Jer 10:19](Jer.10.19); [15:18](Jer.15.18); [30:12](Jer.30.12), [15](Jer.30.15); [Lam 3:12](Lam.3.12); [Mic 1:9](Mic.1.9); [Nah 3:19](Nah.3.19).

Elihu later repeated this accusation ([35:3](Job.35.3); cp. [Ps 73:13](Ps.73.13); [Zeph 1:12](Zeph.1.12); [Mal 3:14](Mal.3.14)), but he misrepresented Job’s words ([Job 9:22-23](Job.9.22-Job.9.23); [21:15](Job.21.15)). Job had actually condemned those who held this view ([21:14-16](Job.21.14-Job.21.16)).

The passage attaches three ideas to the truth that God can do no wrong ([34:10](Job.34.10), [12](Job.34.12)): (1) God pays back all people according to their behavior ([34:11](Job.34.11)); (2) as the Creator, God is not answerable to anyone ([34:13](Job.34.13)); and (3) every living being depends upon God for its existence, and God can withdraw that gift without doing anything wrong ([34:14-15](Job.34.14-Job.34.15); cp. [Rom 9:19-29](Rom.9.19-Rom.9.29)).

**according to their deeds:** Cp. [Ps 62:12](Ps.62.12); [Prov 24:12](Prov.24.12); [Jer 32:19](Jer.32.19); [Ezek 33:20](Ezek.33.20); [Matt 16:27](Matt.16.27); [Rom 2:6](Rom.2.6); [Gal 6:7-8](Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8); [1 Pet 1:17](1Pet.1.17). The ultimate harvest will take place at the end of time ([2 Cor 5:10](2Cor.5.10); [Rev 2:23](Rev.2.23); [22:12](Rev.22.12)).

The implied answer was that **God** could not **govern if he hated justice** (cp. [Rom 3:4-7](Rom.3.4-Rom.3.7); [7:7](Rom.7.7), [13](Rom.7.13); [9:14](Rom.9.14); [Gal 2:17](Gal.2.17); [6:14](Gal.6.14)).
Later, God also asked if Job was **going to condemn the almighty judge** ([Job 40:8](Job.40.8)).

**doesn’t care how great a person may be:** Impartiality flows from God’s justice ([Acts 10:34](Acts.10.34); [Rom 2:11](Rom.2.11); [Gal 2:6](Gal.2.6); [Eph 6:9](Eph.6.9); [Col 3:25](Col.3.25); [1 Pet 1:17](1Pet.1.17)).

The **wicked** might try to hide in **darkness** ([Jer 23:24](Jer.23.24)), but they will fail ([Ps 139:11-12](Ps.139.11-Ps.139.12); cp. [Amos 9:2-3](Amos.9.2-Amos.9.3)). God brings everything to light ([1 Cor 4:5](1Cor.4.5)).
**We don’t set the time:** Elihu rejected Job’s wish for a quick ([21:19](Job.21.19)), published time of **judgment** ([24:1](Job.24.1)).
God knows everything **without asking anyone** ([34:25](Job.34.25)).
**sets up others in their place:** [Dan 2:21](Dan.2.21); [5:28-30](Dan.5.28-Dan.5.30).

When God renders justice **openly**, it leads to proper fear among the wicked ([Deut 21:21](Deut.21.21); [1 Tim 5:20](1Tim.5.20)) and to public rejoicing among the righteous (cp. [Exod 14:30-31](Exod.14.30-Exod.14.31)).
**Why don’t people say?** Elihu was indirectly asking, “Job, why won’t you admit it?”
**deserve the maximum penalty:** Zophar had also said that Job was being punished less than he deserved ([11:6](Job.11.6)).

Elihu attempted to answer his own question ([35:2](Job.35.2)), but his **answer** did not add to what Zophar ([11:8-9](Job.11.8-Job.11.9)), Eliphaz ([22:12](Job.22.12)), Bildad ([25:5-6](Job.25.5-Job.25.6)), and Job ([9:8-10](Job.9.8-Job.9.10)) had already said. Elihu failed to recognize that all sin wrongs God ([Gen 39:9](Gen.39.9); [Matt 25:41-46](Matt.25.41-Matt.25.46); cp. [Prov 19:17](Prov.19.17)).
Elihu echoed and then rejected Job’s words ([9:24](Job.9.24); [12:6-10](Job.12.6-Job.12.10); [21:7-15](Job.21.7-Job.21.15), [17](Job.21.17)).
Elihu echoed his earlier accusation ([34:35](Job.34.35)); later, God would agree ([38:2](Job.38.2)).
**I am a man of great knowledge** (literally *one who is perfect in knowledge is with you*): Elihu was probably claiming to be completely sincere or saying that his logic was flawless.

The biblical principle that God **never takes his eyes off the innocent** ([2 Chr 16:9](2Chr.16.9); [Pss 33:18](Ps.33.18); [34:15](Ps.34.15); [1 Pet 3:12](1Pet.3.12)) answered Job’s frustration about divine surveillance ([Job 7:17-21](Job.7.17-Job.7.21)).

**If they listen and obey God, they will be blessed:** This is a valid biblical principle of repentance (see [11:13-19](Job.11.13-Job.11.19); [22:21-25](Job.22.21-Job.22.25); [Deut 4:30](Deut.4.30); [Jer 7:23](Jer.7.23); [26:13](Jer.26.13)).
**dying from lack of understanding:** See also [4:21](Job.4.21); [Prov 5:23](Prov.5.23); [10:21](Prov.10.21).

The Hebrew *yadin* can mean *he governs* or **he nourishes***,* which parallels **food in abundance** ([38:26](Job.38.26); [Pss 65:9-13](Ps.65.9-Ps.65.13); [104:13-15](Ps.104.13-Ps.104.15), [27-28](Ps.104.27-Ps.104.28)). The more common meaning for *yadin* is “judge,” which would mean that God does all things to bless his people and judge his enemies ([Job 37:11-13](Job.37.11-Job.37.13); [38:22-23](Job.38.22-Job.38.23); see [Gen 6:17](Gen.6.17); [19:24](Gen.19.24); [Exod 9:23-25](Exod.9.23-Exod.9.25); [Josh 10:11-14](Josh.10.11-Josh.10.14); [1 Sam 12:18](1Sam.12.18)).

The Old Testament often associates **thunder** with **God’s voice** ([36:29](Job.36.29), [33](Job.36.33); [37:5](Job.37.5); [38:1](Job.38.1); [Exod 19:16-19](Exod.19.16-Exod.19.19); [Ps 104:7](Ps.104.7)).
**everyone stops working . . . watch his power:** The ending of the agricultural work season gave people time to meditate on God’s providential control.

The same act by God can serve more than one function, such as storms that both destroy enemies and give God’s people victory ([Josh 10](Josh.10.1-Josh.10.43); [Judg 4](Judg.4.1-Judg.4.24); [1 Sam 7:10-11](1Sam.7.10-1Sam.7.11); [Pss 18:7-15](Ps.18.7-Ps.18.15); [105:32-33](Ps.105.32-Ps.105.33)).
The hot **south wind** caused the **sweltering** conditions.
**speak when they are confused?** Or *speak without being swallowed up?* Punishment as severe as death might result from contesting God’s judgment (cp. [13:14](Job.13.14)).

**the mountain of God** (Hebrew *from Zaphon*): In the literature of the ancient city of Ugarit, Zaphon was the northern mountainous abode of Baal; here it figuratively refers to God’s lofty home in the heavens (see [Isa 14:13-14](Isa.14.13-Isa.14.14)).
**cannot imagine the power of the Almighty:** Cp. [11:7](Job.11.7); [26:14](Job.26.14); [Rom 11:33](Rom.11.33); [1 Tim 6:16](1Tim.6.16).

God challenges Job, who acknowledges his inability to judge the moral world by demonstrating his ignorance of the natural world’s cosmic ([38:4-21](Job.38.4-Job.38.21)) and meteorological elements ([38:22-38](Job.38.22-Job.38.38)), animals, and birds ([38:39–39:30](Job.38.39-Job.39.30)).

God challenged Job from out of the **whirlwind**. The Old Testament commonly associates storms with God’s presence ([2 Kgs 2:1](2Kgs.2.1), [11](2Kgs.2.11); [Ezek 1:4](Ezek.1.4); [Nah 1:3](Nah.1.3)). Job finally had an audience with God ([Job 13:22-23](Job.13.22-Job.13.23)).
Finally, **the** **LORD answered Job**. In this final section, the Lord challenges Job’s overreaching self-defense with a display of his works that remind Job of God’s transcendent greatness.

**questions my wisdom:** God’s accusation sounds like a charge made by Eliphaz ([15:2](Job.15.2)) and Elihu ([34:35](Job.34.35); [35:16](Job.35.16)) to which Job eventually admitted guilt ([42:3](Job.42.3)).
The **morning stars** are personified in parallel construction with **the angels** ([1:6](Job.1.6); [2:1](Job.2.1)).
**locked it behind barred gates:** The sea is depicted as a dangerous creature kept under control.
**it is robed in brilliant colors:** The rising sun brings out the colors, shapes, and textures of things.
**you were born before it was all created:** Cp. [Prov 8:25](Prov.8.25). This sarcasm resembles that of Eliphaz ([Job 15:7](Job.15.7)).

**Snow** and **hail** are kept in divine **storehouses** such as those for the deep seas and winds ([Pss 33:7](Ps.33.7); [135:7](Ps.135.7); [Jer 10:13](Jer.10.13); [51:16](Jer.51.16)). God uses these elements as **weapons** ([Job 36:32](Job.36.32); [Isa 30:30](Isa.30.30); [Ezek 13:11-13](Ezek.13.11-Ezek.13.13); [Rev 16:21](Rev.16.21)) in the storms he sends on **the day of battle and war** (e.g., [Josh 10:11](Josh.10.11); [Judg 5:20-21](Judg.5.20-Judg.5.21); [1 Sam 7:10](1Sam.7.10)).

The **east wind** blows off the desert to scorch crops ([Gen 41:6](Gen.41.6), [23](Gen.41.23), [27](Gen.41.27); [Jer 4:11](Jer.4.11); [Jon 4:8](Jonah.4.8)) and dry up seas ([Exod 14:21](Exod.14.21); [Isa 11:15](Isa.11.15)). It is an arid contrast to **the torrents of rain** that cause flooding.

Beneficial **rain to satisfy the parched ground** ([Pss 104:10-11](Ps.104.10-Ps.104.11); [107:35](Ps.107.35); [Isa 35:7](Isa.35.7); [58:11](Isa.58.11)) stands in contrast to both scorching winds ([Job 38:24](Job.38.24)) and flooding rains ([38:25](Job.38.25)).

**heart . . . mind:** These words can also be translated *ibis . . . rooster.* The Egyptians thought the ibis was wise about the flooding of the Nile, the most important seasonal event in Egypt; and Israel’s rabbis thought the rooster could forecast rain or that its crow distinguished day from night. The idea would then be *Who taught the ibis and the rooster?* See also [Ps 51:6](Ps.51.6); [Prov 2:6](Prov.2.6); [Jas 1:5](Jas.1.5), [17](Jas.1.17).

**wild donkey . . . hates** (literally *scorns*) **the noise of the city:** This is the first in a series of animals that scorn others who are their inferiors in some way (cp. [39:18](Job.39.18), [22](Job.39.22); [41:29](Job.41.29)). These images illustrate how God scorns the opposition of a man like Job (see [Ps 2:4](Ps.2.4)).

Now extinct and already rare by Moses’ time, the **wild ox** was the most powerful land animal in early Canaan. This Old Testament symbol of strength ([Num 23:22](Num.23.22); [24:8](Num.24.8); [Deut 33:17](Deut.33.17); [Pss 29:6](Ps.29.6); [92:10](Ps.92.10)) was never **tamed** (cp. [Gen 1:28](Gen.1.28); [9:2](Gen.9.2); [Ps 8:5-6](Ps.8.5-Ps.8.6)).
In the ancient Near East, the **ostrich** had a reputation as a bird that God had **deprived** of **wisdom.**

The ostrich is a symbol of neglect for her **young** ([Lam 4:3](Lam.4.3)) because she (1) **lays her eggs on top of the earth***;* (2) appears to leave her eggs to **die** when a predator approaches them (although she is probably attempting to lure the predator away from the nest); and (3) lays her eggs with several other hens in one nest, so most of the eggs are **not her own**.
**passes** (literally *scorns*) **the swiftest horse with its rider:** See [39:7](Job.39.7), [22](Job.39.22); [41:29](Job.41.29).
The **ram’s horn** was sounded in combat to call for the charge ([Josh 6:4-6](Josh.6.4-Josh.6.6)).
**Where there’s a carcass, there you’ll find it**—feeding on the remains ([Ezek 39:17-19](Ezek.39.17-Ezek.39.19); [Matt 24:28](Matt.24.28); [Luke 17:37](Luke.17.37)).
The Greek Old Testament omits this conclusion to God’s first speech.

Job’s brief and humble response does not acknowledge guilt, but it does admit his insignificance ([40:4](Job.40.4)). He had previously thought that he could approach God like a prince ([31:37](Job.31.37)) or even cross-examine him ([13:22-23](Job.13.22-Job.13.23)).
**I am nothing** (cp. [42:6](Job.42.6)): Job was not repenting from sin; like Abraham, he recognized his unworthiness ([Gen 18:27](Gen.18.27)).
Job had asked his comforters to **cover** their **mouth** to acknowledge shock ([21:5](Job.21.5)); here he does so himself in reaction to his own rash words.
Job had **nothing more to say***;* he had no further charges against God, nor would he make a rebuttal.
The Lord repeated his earlier challenge (see [38:1-3](Job.38.1-Job.38.3)).
Job’s words ([10:7](Job.10.7); [27:2](Job.27.2); [31:35-37](Job.31.35-Job.31.37)) had angered Elihu ([32:2](Job.32.2); [34:5](Job.34.5)); now God himself challenged them.

Job could not do God’s work of humbling the proud ([Isa 2:11-12](Isa.2.11-Isa.2.12), [17](Isa.2.17); [Jas 4:6](Jas.4.6); [1 Pet 5:5-6](1Pet.5.5-1Pet.5.6)) apart from God’s authority ([Mal 4:3](Mal.4.3); [Rom 16:20](Rom.16.20)).

Following a list of natural animals ([39:1-30](Job.39.1-Job.39.30)), God described Behemoth ([40:15-24](Job.40.15-Job.40.24)) and Leviathan ([41:1-34](Job.41.1-Job.41.34)) as creatures that man cannot tame. Job couldn’t tame the wild donkey or ox ([39:5-12](Job.39.5-Job.39.12)), let alone Behemoth and Leviathan ([40:15-24](Job.40.15-Job.40.24)), but God created them and could control them, and Job had to acknowledge it ([41:2](Job.41.2)).

Here **Behemoth** seems to be a natural creature: (1) It is an animal that God **made***,* just as he made Job ([40:15](Job.40.15)); (2) it is not a dreadful predator but **eats grass like an ox** ([40:15](Job.40.15)); and (3) it is in a poem describing God’s creation of the natural order, rather than in a mythological story of the world’s formation. Most commentators identify Behemoth with the hippopotamus, a huge, grass-eating animal ([40:15-19](Job.40.15-Job.40.19)) that lies in the river among the lotus plants and reeds ([40:21](Job.40.21)). Like the wild ox, Behemoth is powerful ([40:16-18](Job.40.16-Job.40.18), [24](Job.40.24); [39:11](Job.39.11)), yet is essentially peaceful ([40:20-23](Job.40.20-Job.40.23)).

Unlike the peaceful Behemoth ([40:15-24](Job.40.15-Job.40.24)), **Leviathan** was menacing (see also [3:8](Job.3.8); [Pss 74:14](Ps.74.14); [104:26](Ps.104.26); [Isa 27:1](Isa.27.1)). Most commentators identify Leviathan with the crocodile, with its terrible jaws ([Job 41:14](Job.41.14)) and armored hide ([41:15-17](Job.41.15-Job.41.17), [23](Job.41.23)), thrashing the water ([41:31-32](Job.41.31-Job.41.32)). But Leviathan is a fire-breathing dragon ([41:18-21](Job.41.18-Job.41.21)) that wraps its coils around the sun to cause an eclipse ([3:8-9](Job.3.8-Job.3.9)). The background for Leviathan is the seven-headed sea monster that represents chaos in ancient Near Eastern mythology. In the biblical record, this unruly maritime monster is a frequent biblical image for chaos and wickedness, whose head the Lord crushes ([Ps 74:14](Ps.74.14); [Isa 27:1](Isa.27.1); cp. [Job 9:13](Job.9.13); [26:12](Job.26.12); [Ps 89:9-10](Ps.89.9-Ps.89.10); [Isa 30:7](Isa.30.7); [51:9](Isa.51.9)). Later in the Bible, Satan is linked to the ancient serpent ([Gen 3](Gen.3.1-Gen.3.24)) and unruly dragon ([Rev 12:9](Rev.12.9); [20:2](Rev.20.2)), whose head Christ and his followers crush ([Rom 16:20](Rom.16.20)).

Job understood the message of God’s speeches: **I know that you can do anything**. Nothing is too hard for God ([Gen 18:14](Gen.18.14); [Jer 32:17](Jer.32.17); [Matt 19:26](Matt.19.26)) and nothing can stop his plan ([Job 23:13](Job.23.13); [Isa 14:27](Isa.14.27); [46:10](Isa.46.10)). Job realized how unlike God he was.
**now I have seen you:** Up to this point, Job had not seen God (see [23:8](Job.23.8)); now, like Isaiah, he had been in God’s presence and was overwhelmed by God’s holiness ([Isa 6:1](Isa.6.1)).

**Eliphaz the Temanite** was the spokesman for the friends, which probably indicates his seniority. Eliphaz had falsely implied that his advice originated in prophetic visions ([4:12-16](Job.4.12-Job.4.16)); now God did speak to him, but not to affirm his message.

Unlike his three friends (cp. [13:7-10](Job.13.7-Job.13.10)), Job had **spoken accurately** about God. Job’s blunt questions were better suited to arriving at the truth about God than the friends’ superficial orthodox doctrine.

The Lord made Job the mediator that Job had hoped to find for himself ([9:33](Job.9.33); [16:19-21](Job.16.19-Job.16.21); [19:25](Job.19.25)) and that Elihu desired to be ([32:1–37:24](Job.32.1-Job.37.24)).
**go to my servant Job:** God wanted Job’s friends to be reconciled with Job before they presented their offerings ([Matt 5:23-24](Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24)).
**My servant Job will pray for you***;* he had also prayed for his children ([1:5](Job.1.5); cp. [Jas 5:16](Jas.5.16); [1 Jn 5:16](1John.5.16)).
When **the** **LORD accepted Job’s prayer***,* it ironically fulfilled Eliphaz’s promise ([Job 22:26-30](Job.22.26-Job.22.30)).
Job’s **fortunes** probably included his health ([42:16-17](Job.42.16-Job.42.17)). God created humans in order to bless them, not curse them.

Although Job was restored, he still needed to be **consoled** and **comforted** for the loss of his children. Following Job’s own earlier practice ([4:4](Job.4.4); [16:5](Job.16.5)), his family and **former friends** took up where the three other friends left off ([2:11](Job.2.11); cp. [2 Cor 7:6](2Cor.7.6)).

The **gift of money** was not so much charity to provide a financial basis for Job’s restored fortune as it was to honor and seek the favor of an influential man (e.g., [Prov 18:16](Prov.18.16)), and perhaps even to assuage disfavor (e.g., [Gen 32:20](Gen.32.20); [33:10](Gen.33.10); [43:11](Gen.43.11); [1 Sam 25:27](1Sam.25.27)).

A **gold ring** was worn in a woman’s nose ([Gen 24:47](Gen.24.47); [Prov 11:22](Prov.11.22); [Isa 3:21](Isa.3.21)) or on the ears of either men or women ([Gen 35:4](Gen.35.4); [Exod 32:2-3](Exod.32.2-Exod.32.3); [Judg 8:24](Judg.8.24)).
When God **blessed** Job, it ironically fulfilled Bildad’s promise ([8:7](Job.8.7)).
The beautiful names of Job’s new daughters spoke of Job’s renewed and pleasant good fortunes.
**Jemimah** means “dove” (see [Song 2:14](Song.2.14)).
**Keziah** means “cassia” or “cinnamon flower” (see [Ps 45:8](Ps.45.8)).
**Keren-happuch** means “horn of antimony,” which refers to a lustrous container for cosmetics.

**their father put them into his will:** Daughters normally inherited only when there were no male heirs ([Num 27](Num.27.1-Num.27.23); [36](Num.36.1-Num.36.13)). Perhaps Job’s unusual action expressed his superabundant prosperity; only a wealthy man could afford to pass some of his wealth to the families into which his daughters would marry.

**140 years** was twice the normal life span ([Ps 90:10](Ps.90.10)). If the analogy of double restoration holds ([Job 42:10](Job.42.10)), Job might have been 70 already and then lived another 140 years. A life span of 210 years would not be out of keeping with the patriarchal setting of the book (see [Gen 25:7](Gen.25.7); [35:28](Gen.35.28); [47:28](Gen.47.28); [50:26](Gen.50.26); [Deut 34:7](Deut.34.7); [Josh 24:29](Josh.24.29)).
**living to see four generations of his children and grandchildren:** Job’s blessing extended to watching his multigenerational family grow ([Gen 50:23](Gen.50.23); [Ps 128:6](Ps.128.6)).

Like Abraham and Isaac, who also died at a ripe old age ([Gen 25:8](Gen.25.8); [35:29](Gen.35.29)), Job **lived a long, full life***,* fulfilling Eliphaz’s promise ([Job 5:26](Job.5.26)), which was based on God’s general promise ([Deut 6:2](Deut.6.2); [Ps 91:16](Ps.91.16)).

At the end of the book, the Greek Old Testament adds a note declaring that Job will rise from the dead at the resurrection. It goes on to provide information about where and when Job and his descendants lived.
